The matter I should like to take up with the Prime Minister is not along the same lines as the one which has just been discussed. Strictly speaking, Mr. Chairman,
I am perhaps not in order, but in view of its importance and in view of the fact that it concerns the Prime Minister I hope he will allow me to bring it to his attention at this time.
This matter has to do with a suggestion the Prime Minister has made, I believe, on more than one occasion concerning the census and the fact that an individual should not be required to state his ethnic origin. I thought 

perhaps I might say just one word in connection with it today. I should like, as objectively as possible, to state the reasons why I should like to bring it to the Prime Minister's attention. The matter is one which has been of particular interest to my compatriots in Quebec, and also in other provinces in Canada.
It has seemed to them that if that suggestion were put into effect it might well work not only a hardship but great difficulties. I know the Prime Minister's attention has been drawn to this subject by a number of organizations across Canada. For instance, I believe that la federation des associations de parents et d'instituteurs de langue frangaise d'Ontario have written the Prime Minister, as have l'association canadienne-frangaise d'education d'Ontario, and the point they made and the point which I should like to reiterate on their behalf is that it is not felt by them that the leaving in of the ethnic origin is a matter which will be conducive to disunity. On the contrary, they feel that it will be conducive to unity. They say, and have so asserted, that they are quite favourable to union and unity of all Canadians of all origins, but always in diversity. They say that what makes the strength, grandeur and originality of our country is the respect for the diversity of origins and various cultures which develop loyalty to the country and to the crown.
They also make the point that the slightest attempt or the slightest infringement of the spirit of the constitution and of the program they have set out for their people would be, in their opinion, a source of difficulty. They go on and state that they have in the past relied a great deal upon information of the ethnical origins of their people from one end of the country to the other. There are, as the Prime Minister knows, associations like the ones I have mentioned in practically every province of Canada save perhaps one or two.
While I am not speaking for all of them, I think I speak for the group that brought this matter to my attention. They state that the information they get from the national census has been of tremendous assistance and importance to them in the development of our traditions, our customs, our culture, and in a comparison of these things with other groups across Canada.
Then I should like to state that in a letter which was addressed to the Prime Minister by l'association canadienne-frangaise d'education d'Ontario they point with particular emphasis to a paragraph contained in the report of the royal commission on arts, letters and sciences, which can be found at page 4. It is difficult for me to translate it without more

time so if the Prime Minister will allow me to do so I should like to read it as it is. It is as follows:
(Translation):
That it is desirable that the Canadian people should know as much as possible about their country, its history and traditions; and about their national life and common achievements; that it is in the national interest to give encouragement to institutions which express national feeling, promote common understanding and add to the variety and richness of Canadian life, rural as well as urban.
(Text):
From those two statements, the one which I took from la federation des associations de parents et d'instituteurs de langue frangaise d'Ontario and the other from the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences in Canada, it would appear that valuable information would be taken away from these groups if in the future it were not possible to obtain the ethnic origin of the citizens who are registered under the act. In making that statement I speak, I am sure, not only for many of the members of the opposition but equally for many of the members of my hon. friend's party. I know I have had the opportunity to speak not to all of them, of course, but to some of them, and I think they feel as strongly as I do and as strongly as these associations on the matter.
I do not want to overstate the case, because the Prime Minister has been good enough to listen to what I have had to say notwithstanding the fact that perhaps I am not strictly in order. All I want to do is state that while this matter may not be determined for some years, nevertheless I appeal to the Prime Minister to give consideration to what I have said and to the representations that have been made by these associations. I feel that he will do so.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a similar question on the royal commission covered by this particular item, the royal commission on price spreads in food products. I should like to know how it is getting on and when it is likely to report. I know that once a commission gets into this particular subject of price spreads it can go on and on and on. I realize that the members of this commission are men of intelligence and industry, and that they are doing admirable work, but I was wondering what limitation the government is putting on this study and when it is likely to be brought to a conclusion. I recall in the thirties starting off as secretary of a parliamentary committee on price spreads. Incidentally, that committee was a parliamentary committee which began its work in an atmosphere of excitement and partisanship and which was transformed into a royal commission when it worked more constructively-an interesting precedent. I know that when this committee began its work it felt it could be completed within a few months, but it went on for two years.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
As the hon. Leader of the Opposition says, this is a very difficult assignment which has been given to this royal commission, and the Leader of the Opposition speaks with authority beyond that possessed by any other member of the committee, for when Mr. Bennett set up the royal commission on price spreads the hon. gentleman was the secretary of that body and he has full knowledge of the difficulties of investigation and the ramifications of the problems.
The research program conducted by the staff of the commission, with assistance from government departments, began along three lines:
(a)	Analysis of price data and measurement of over-all aspects of the commission's problem, including changes in consumer expenditures on food, changes in receipts of primary producers from the sale of food products, and changes in the over-all cost of processing and distributing food products over the period from 1949 to 1958.
(b)	Studies of particular aspects of the marketing of food products in relation to price spreads, including transportation, storage, packaging, advertising, wages and productivity, the effects of co-operatives and marketing boards, and the nature of competition and profitability of firms engaged in food marketing.
(c)	Commodity studies, covering those that make up a large part of the consumers' expenditures on food and those that are most important in the incomes of producers.
I know of no commission which is more important than this one so far as agriculture and fisheries are concerned for, after all, the primary producer, the farmer and the fisherman, has certain costs which are basic, and the larger the share of the consumer dollar

expended for the particular commodities which becomes available to the primary producer the better the return to the farmer and the fisherman. This is one of the major facets in agricultural policy; in other words, that within the limits of a fair and reasonable return for the intermediary, the wholesaler and the retailer, assurance should be given that the producer shall not suffer as a result of improvident and excessive advantage to intermediaries between the producer and the ultimate consumer.
So important is this that I feel that the members of this commission have a most responsible and exacting task. Over the years this type of investigation has been requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, by the farmer's union and also by fish producers. I cannot say when the report will be available. The commission is applying itself very diligently but I am unable to give the hon. gentleman even an approximate date. In this case I was of the opinion that a matter of three or four months would pretty well cover the responsibility. I was assured by the chairman that my views in that regard were too optimistic because of the ramifications of the problem and the various facets that are faced from day to day. I can only say they will make a report at the earliest possible date.

Mr. Chairman, it is certain that the problem to which the Prime Minister has referred, namely of reducing the spread between the prices paid to the primary producer and those charged to the retailer, is a very important one. Agricultural producers are looking to this royal commission in the hope that following its report and the subsequent action flowing out of the report the trend which has been prevalent for some years will be reversed. The trend to which I refer is that which has meant the producer has received a decreasing part of the consumer dollar spent on food. There is no doubt that the whole field into which this commission is inquiring is of great importance but the inquiry is of importance itself only if it leads to some concrete action. We shall look with interest to the report that is made and we shall look with even more interest to the action taken following the report.
I do not believe it is necessary to wait for the report to do something in the interests of the agricultural producers of this country. I refer, of course, to the necessity of improving the prices that are paid to producers. Following the report that may be made by the royal commission I believe the government should consider the whole
57071-3-246i
Supply-Privy Council question of price controls. While the government does not provide a system of price controls at the retail level, nevertheless every positive action it may take by way of price legislation to help producers is by way of management or control or in other ways influencing the prices paid to the producers. I refer, of course, to the Agricultural Stabilization Act, to initial payments that are made by the Canadian wheat board and to other measures that are adopted from time to time.
We shall await the report of the royal commission with interest and shall press the government for whatever action the commission may recommend that may bring about this very desirable result. Important as the report will be it will require subsequent action to meet the important problem that farmers face of receiving year after year a constantly diminishing share of the consumer dollar.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to stop my own estimates going through but I do believe that the actions taken by this government have indicated its desire to assure agriculture of a fair share of the national income. The steps taken so far have been progressive steps. The first was to provide financial assistance through cash advances and that has worked out exceptionally well with little or no loss to the state. The second step was the broad plan of a price stabilization establishment in respect of various agricultural products. I am not exhausting what has been done when I mention as a third step the setting up of this royal commission which was established because of the general request through the years on the part of farm organizations for this investigation. We do not set up royal commissions for the purpose of making findings upon which no action will in any way be taken.
I would not have said that were it not for the fact the hon. gentleman talked about price controls. I do not wish to leave any misapprehension in his mind on that question. I am one of those who believe that the price controls effective in time of war because of the mobilization of all the people in the state would be less than successful in times of a reasonably free economy. I know the hon. gentleman will not misunderstand me when I bring to his attention the fact that the government of Saskatchewan in 1946 brought in legislation which was to be established upon proclamation whereby the prices of various products would be fixed by the state and any one failing to adhere to the prices fixed by the board set up for that purpose would find himself subject to a penalty or in the alternative subject to a jail

Supply-Privy Council sentence. But that legislation was never proclaimed within Saskatchewan because if it had been, as I said on one previous occasion, there would have been only two classes of people in the province, those in jail and those waiting to get in after the others got out.
I know the hon. gentleman did not have that in mind when he spoke about fixing prices because what the state can do is to provide the means through fair and reasonable legislation whereby the farmer and other primary producers shall be placed in a position in which they will not be subject to unjust and unfair competition and that their prices shall bear a fair relationship to their costs.
I am not going to argue the case of the stabilization legislation but that was the basis of that legislation. I can tell the hon. member that in so far as this royal commission is concerned I hope that out of a multiplicity of representations will come reasonable and fair conclusions upon which parliament can act.
I give him that assurance. I was hoping those recommendations might come earlier. As a matter of fact it was the farm organizations that brought to my attention the fact it would take much longer than the comparatively short period I had in mind to secure a full and accurate summary of the situation to the end that legislative enactment might be based thereon.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Prime
Minister has outlined some of the things the government has done by way of an agricultural program. The program of cash advances is one I advocated for many years along with other hon. members of this group. I take second place to no one, not even the Prime Minister, as an advocate of that type of policy. I share with him the general satisfaction he felt that the program of cash advances within the conception of the act has worked out reasonably well and that the excuses given by the former administration as to why this could not be done through the existing machinery, namely the Canadian wheat board, were not in fact valid and that the wheat board has been able to handle this legislation.
However, I think we should all keep cash advances in perspective as to what they really do. During the fall months they enable farmers to get an advance on expected sales of grain over the 12-month period but apart from the saving in the interest rate generally speaking they do not add to the economic position of the farmer. They do not increase his real income over a one-year period except to the extent that he is able to make a saving with respect to interest on the money obtained through cash advances.

The Prime Minister referred to the government's price stabilization policy. As far as I am concerned the price stabilization policy and the floors established thereunder have not been such as to give the farmer a fair and reasonable return or provide him with adequate parity prices as promised by the government in two election campaigns.
I have said that in order to protect the producer there must be a system of price controls by way of supports for those products that the producer is engaged in producing and marketing. I certainly stand by that statement. The Prime Minister has said that he is not in favour of the type of price controls used during the war but it is certainly a form of price control to establish a floor price for butter. It is certainly a measure of price control to say that a deficiency payment will be paid on soybeans in order to bring about a certain result. Every action that the government takes to stabilize agricultural prices is in itself a measure of control over those prices.
I have said that the government's agricultural price stabilization policy has been a disappointment to me and members of the C.C.F. and farmers generally. Although I do not have the quotation on my desk, I can bring as my witness Mr. Turnbull, second vice-president of the Saskatchewan farmers union and a member of the advisory committee under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. He has said that the act has not increased the economic welfare of the average farmer as he would like to see it improved. He has gone much further and has said that in the main what the act has done is to help the very large farmers. These are the comments of this farm union official.
We shall await with interest the report of the royal commission and any subsequent action the government may take but as far as I am concerned I want to make it crystal clear that since June 21, 1957, no adequate improvement has taken place in the position of the agricultural industry. In particular I refer to the final payments made on wheat a few weeks ago which were the smallest made for many years. I know that the Prime Minister has often said that he has under active consideration further measures to aid the grain producers of western Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing to the committee the estimates of the Department of Fisheries I first want to point out that the estimates have been very carefully and thoroughly considered by the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the members of that committee on their very
Supply-Fisheries
fine, constructive attitude towards the problems of the Department of Fisheries and for the contribution they made in the consideration of the estimates of the department. I may say that they showed complete knowledge of the fishing industry in the whole of Canada. That is not surprising because the committee had on it members of parliament representing all the major fishing areas of the country and many of them at one time or another have been directly engaged in that industry. Therefore I can say without reservation that all parties in the house were extremely well represented on that committee by members who contributed a great deal to its proceedings. For that reason my remarks will be brief but there are a few points I should like to mention which I feel would be of interest to the membership of this committee.
To begin with, I should like to say a word about the economic situation of the industry at the present time. So far as the economic situation of the fishery generally is concerned, the three major factors are production, price to the fisherman and export markets. Although the fisheries are carried out in all areas at all times during the year, the months of greatest production are July, August and September. It is, therefore, too early to state definitively how production will stand this year. But the figures we have indicate that across the country catches will be up to those of recent years. In so far as individual species are concerned, of course, the catch in some cases will be higher, while in others it will be lower.
One of our greatest worries arose out of the very disappointing cod trap fishery in Newfoundland this year and now because of a failure of the squid fishery it is a difficult problem to secure adequate supplies of bait to keep the cod fishery going throughout the fall. I am happy to be able to announce we have found a source of herring bait at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, which should help materially to meet this need. While herring is not as desirable as the local squid bait, it has always been used extensively throughout the maritime provinces. We hope it will be a reasonably satisfactory substitute for any shortage of squid which there may be in Newfoundland.
On the Pacific coast, we are just now entering the main salmon season. All indications point to an exceptionally large pack, particularly of the valuable sockeye species. The catch in most of the other major fisheries has been well up to average in all areas. Prices to fishermen are, of course, related to the supply situation and to the demand, both at home and abroad. In Canada, while we are still

Supply-Fisheries
relatively light fish eaters in comparison with other countries, there has been a slow but gradual upward trend in per capita consumption. The department is continuing its efforts through its consumer service, and by other means, to keep this movement going. Demand in the United States, our principal market of fresh and frozen fish, has also been strong. The current market position for these forms of fish is one example of low stocks and gradually increasing prices. For example, the price of frozen cod fillets is three cents per pound higher and that for frozen haddock fillets five cents per pound higher than a year ago in the major wholesale market at Boston.
The expected high salmon pack this year will coincide with a higher allocation of dollars by the United Kingdom, our principal market. However, it may well be that some of the expected large 1958 production will have to be carried over into the 1959 marketing year when supplies are expected to be much shorter.
Mention has been made on several occasions of the salt fish market problem. As I have indicated, there has been a very disappointing production in Newfoundland this year. Thus, while supplies will be lower there should be no great difficulty in marketing the reduced output. The large and valuable lobster fishery of the Atlantic coast provinces again gives every promise of a satisfactory year.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am fully satisfied with all aspects of the fishery, and to suggest that there are not many old and new problems confronting the Industry and the department. One of our major problems is that of ensuring good [DOT]quality of all types of fish at all times. This is a very complex problem when we consider the diversity of the industry across the country and the perishability of the product. The government role in this field is essentially one of education and inspection, and we are stepping up our activities in both these fields. The inspection service is expanding its scope so that the consumer may be able to obtain fresh and frozen fish products inspected to conform to high quality specifications being prepared by this department in consultation with other government services and the fishing industry. The governments of the provinces have indicated their co-operation and approval of our entry into this field, so that this additional service will be truly national in extent. The government of the province of Quebec has requested that this department administer the inspection of fish and fish products for that province and steps are presently being taken to comply with this request.

Industrial development is another service of the department which has been expanding its activities in the past year. This service is designed to work with all branches of the industry in bringing new techniques into operation. The government's role here is one of testing, experimenting and demonstrating as well as giving encouragement to fishermen and the industry generally. In this field, we co-operate also with the provincial departments concerned and an Atlantic coast federal-provincial fisheries committee has been set up to provide for close liaison and full co-ordination in this field. This committee will also deal with other problems of mutual concern.
In the field of research, the fisheries research board is the operating agency and its expenditures are included in the estimates now before this committee. The activities of this organization cover not only biological, technological and oceanographic research but also there is a special unit based in Montreal concerned with developments in the Arctic area. This unit is endeavouring to learn more about the availability and life habits of fish and other marine animals in our vast northern waters.
One of the special fields of research which has become more and more urgent is that associated with hydroelectric developments in our major fish rivers. Engineering and biological studies in this field are being carried out, not only by the Department of Fisheries research board but also by such organizations as the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. In addition, close liaison is maintained with the technical staffs of the United States fisheries agencies regarding progress and development in this important field. It should be of interest to note that expenditures for these studies by Canadian agencies in the Pacific area in the current year will be in excess of $700,000. The expenditures by both Canadian and United States agencies will total over $2 million. These totals refer only to expenditures for experimental devices and research and do not include capital expenditures for fish protective devices.
The problems under investigation range from laboratory studies of the basic behaviour patterns of juvenile salmon to large-scale field tests of devices for deflecting seaward migrating salmon into by-passes which will provide a safe passage around power dams.
Earlier I mentioned the difficulty we are having in securing adequate supplies of bait in Newfoundland arising out of the failure of the squid fishery in that province this year. I should like to point out that the Newfoundland bait service, which was taken over by

the federal department at the time of union, was designed to meet fishing conditions in Newfoundland as they existed prior to the last war. Since that time, and particularly since union, there have been many changes not only in the types of fishing being carried on in that province but also in the areas where fishing activities are of major importance. It, therefore, became necessary to reorganize the service to meet present-day conditions. Included in this year's estimates, particularly in the supplementary estimates, is provision for strengthening not only our freezing and storing facilities but also our distribution facilities so that as bait is secured we will be able to more adequately meet the needs of the fishermen in all parts of Newfoundland.
There are several other fields of activity where the Department of Fisheries and the research board are changing the emphasis to meet changing conditions in the fishery.
For example, we are undertaking to assist and expand the oyster fishery of the Atlantic coast through the development of better methods of providing seed oysters. On the Pacific coast and in the salmon producing areas of the Atlantic coast we are also undertaking major experiments in the improvement of spawning and rearing conditions, not only in the natural rivers but also in the provision of artificial spawning areas.
I have touched on only a few of the problems and plans of the department and the fisheries research board but, as I indicated in my opening remarks, we have already in the marine and fisheries committee given these estimates very thorough consideration and I trust that the committee, for the most part, will realize that that has been the case. In the committee on marine and fisheries I was delighted to find that there were no serious criticisms of the activities of my department. For this situation I take no personal credit but I should like at this time to pay a passing tribute to a very fine and dedicated group of public servants who are giving their full time and attention to the problems of the fishing industry as employees of my department. To them belongs the credit.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity publicly to congratulate the minister in the name of the members on this side of the house of the official opposition on the honour which was bestowed upon him by Mount Allison University on Saturday last. In introducing his estimates the minister stated that the fisheries estimates were considered by the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I agree with the minister that
Supply-Fisheries
the members of this committee took a constructive attitude in discussing the problems affecting the fishing industry. In dealing with the economic situation of the industry the minister stated that so far this year the catches are well up to those of previous years. At this point I must mention the fact that especially on the Atlantic coast the number of fishermen engaged this year in fishing operations is much larger than that in previous years. If present economic conditions are to prevail in the future it is expected that this number will increase in future years. In passing I wish to remark that this situation might be contrary to a part of the report of the Gordon commission which asserted that the number of fishermen would decrease year after year.
We were also pleased to hear from the minister that the prices of fish were satisfactory. He mentioned the prices of cod fillets and haddock fillets which were much higher on the United States market than they were at this time last year. We are also pleased to realize that at least some of the benefits of this increase in price have been passed along to the fishermen as the primary producers.
The members of this committee, Mr. Chairman, realize the importance of the fishing industry to the economy of our country. In the brief remarks which I intend to make at this time it is not my intention to criticize the Department of Fisheries but rather, if possible, to offer constructive suggestions directed toward improving the situation of our Canadian fishermen. We all know that the fishing industry is one of the oldest industries of our country. It has been part of Canada's pattern for over 400 years. The prolific fishing grounds of the North Atlantic led to the discovery of the North American continent. It is also of importance to realize that last year the total catch amounted to over 2 billion pounds having a commercial value of $200 million. It affected over 80,000 Canadian fishermen and a large number of workers in fish processing plants.
I also want to take advantage of the opportunity offered at this time to express my appreciation for the co-operation which we receive from the officers and staff of the department and of the fisheries research board. We understand the difficulties which are encountered by some of the officials in the field, especially those in the protection service. At this point I should like to repeat what I said when I first spoke in this house in 1953, namely that I should like to see the protective officers of the fisheries department giving more time and attention to the education of the fishermen. The protective officer could be more effective if he were to spend

Supply-Fisheries
more time at the end of the fishing wharf talking to fishermen when they return from the fishing grounds, explaining to them how to take care of their fish and showing them that it is to their own interest to protect the fisheries.
I was also pleased to hear the minister mention the fact that the inspection service of his department was expanding year after year and that the inspection of fresh fish, which this year will be on a voluntary basis, will be applied on a national scale.
I have made the suggestion that the protective officers should spend more time in educating the fishermen. At this point I want to say a few words about an education program which has been in existence in the department for some years but which should be extended. We realize that the ordinary elementary Schools have not personnel qualified or trained to be practical and to give to the fishermen the education which they need in order to carry on with their fishing operations. The modernization of the fishing fleet in recent years make it much more urgent for a new concept of this major problem.
The extensive research which has been carried on by scientists of the fisheries research board has led to the introduction of new fishing methods and new techniques resulting in greater output and greater production. However, I repeat that more emphasis should be given to the practical application on a commercial basis of the findings of the research board. This can be done only by actual and on the spot demonstrations so that the fishermen can see for themselves and be convinced of the advantages offered by those new methods or techniques.
During the deliberations in the standing committee on marine and fisheries we were pleased to hear from the minister that a federal-provincial Atlantic fisheries committee had been formed. We welcome this new committee which we understand will have as its main duty that of showing to the fishermen in a practical way the findings of the research board.
If I recall correctly, during the period 1937 to 1947 a study was carried out by the fisheries research board of the federal department in co-operation with the Atlantic provinces, and the province of Newfoundland. Notwithstanding this lengthy experiment, in many areas of the Atlantic coast our herring fishermen are still using the same outmoded methods used by their great-grandfathers. I hope the fisheries research board will make the new methods if any known to the fishermen.
I understand that this summer in my own constituency at Caraquet, for instance, they
IMr. Robichaud.]
are trying to prove the advantages and the possibility of the mid-water trawl for fishing herring, and I wish to say to the minister that if an experiment of this kind is to be truly effective it should be carried out during the entire fishing season. It should commence on April 15 and the fishermen with this new gear should look and fish for herring all through a whole season up to at least October 15. I was in my constituency about ten days ago and up to that time I understand that nothing has been done to establish whether or not it was possible to introduce a system of mid-water trawling for herring in the bay of Chaleur.
We have in Canada many schools, colleges and universities for agriculture; we have such institutions in probably all our provinces. We have, however, only two schools for fisheries, the school for fisheries at Ste. Anne-de-la-Pocatiere and the fishery school at Grande Riviere which is operated by the government of Quebec. I would again ask the minister, and through him his department, to give serious consideration to providing further and more effective assistance to our universities, especially to colleges or universities in the provinces in which fishing is one of the main industries, in order to train our fishermen to use and take full advantage of modern methods of fishing.
At this point I would like to deal with a problem which is of great concern to east coast fishermen. I refer to a support price or floor price for fish. At this very moment I realize our fishermen on the Atlantic coast may be receiving prices which are perhaps more attractive than those which they received at this time last year, but they have no guarantee that such prices will be maintained in the years to come. During the federal election campaign the Prime Minister himself made statements which I think should be placed on the record. In addressing a meeting in Charlottetown on February 27 the Prime Minister made certain statements which were reported in the Toronto Star of February 28 as follows:
He told the audience of more than 1,100 which crammed the hall above the Roloway bowling club that the government was now considering providing the same kind of price support legislation for the fishing industry as it had for the farmers, although he acknowledged there were "difficulties in the way".
The Halifax Chronicle-Herald of March 25, 1958 contained a report of statements said to have been made by the Prime Minister on March 24 as follows:
This government, he told the audience, was moving to stabilize prices for farm produce, and consideration is now being given to bring about "the application", on a similar basis, of this measure as it affects fish products.

The Halifax Chronicle-Herald of March 26 reported the following statement made at Yarmouth on March 25:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker today promised federal price supports under fish and a firm stand on protection of Canadian inshore fisheries against foreign trawlers.
And further on it says:
The Prime Minister said "We want to do that if you want it."
I wish the Prime Minister were now in his seat, because I would ask him what he meant by those words, "We want to do that if you want it."
The same article quotes the Prime Minister as saying that the Conservative government is taking the first strong step in the matter. The Prime Minister was at that time proposing that the national jurisdiction be extended 12 miles offshore in regard to fisheries, but I will deal with that particular point in a few moments.
I have in my hand a 1957 report on primary industry studies undertaken by the Department of Fisheries economic service, concerning the operations of modern long liners and draggers on the Atlantic seaboard. It is said that these operations have been going on during the past seven years and this service has given the industry and the department most valuable information. I wish to congratulate the department upon its initiative in this regard. In order to arrive at the figures, the official of the department in charge took 125 boats, divided among the different Atlantic provinces, in order to get an average of the landings, the returns and the cost of operation for these fishermen in the year 1957.
The report shows that in Nova Scotia the 50-foot to 60-foot dragger had a deficit of $2,059; the same type of dragger in New Brunswick had a deficit of $495; in Prince Edward Island the deficit was $1,070; and in Quebec $1,767. The same report shows that in order to break even the fishermen in the different provinces should have had a minimum price for their fish and this price varied from 2.7 for a 45-foot to 50-foot dragger in Nova Scotia; 2.5 for a 50-foot to 60-foot dragger in New Brunswick; 3.074 for a 50-foot to 60-foot dragger in Prince Edward Island; and 2.0 for a 50-foot to 60-foot dragger in the province of Quebec. I also have a report for 1956, and there is very little difference in the deficit encountered by the fishermen and the average price received by them for their fish.
I have, in addition, a statement made by Mr. C. E. Desourdy, general manager of the Quebec united fishermen, and I would like to quote from the review published by the fisheries school at Ste. Anne-de-la-Pocatiere 57071-3-247
Supply-Fisheries
with respect to what he had to say on a floor price for fish:
(Translation):
The federal government must find some means of enforcing that legislation which provides for a support price on fish. Some hopes may be held in this regard although no definite decision has been reached as yet.
(Text):
The federal government must find means to introduce legislation to establish price support for fish. On this subject we may have certain hopes, but nothing definite has been decided to date. The cod fishery of the Atlantic provinces and of the Atlantic coast is very important. It represents practically 45 per cent of the total catch and it is valued at between $30 and $35 million a year. Part of this catch is processed into salt cod for the Mediterranean and Caribbean market and a small percentage goes to the United States market. A large percentage of the catch is filleted and shipped fresh or frozen either to the domestic market or to the United States. We have been told at different times that 70 per cent of our total catch is exported and that 65 per cent of these exports go to the United States market. Unless our fishermen are guaranteed a minimum price of three cents a pound for fresh cod landed it is impossible for them to carry on. They cannot operate at a deficit year after year. This is a responsibility of the government. It has been promised to them that ways and means will be found to protect them by a guaranteed price of at least three cents a pound.
At this point I should like to say a few words about the information and educational service branch of the department. The duty of this branch is to bring to the attention of the Canadian public the importance of the fisheries to our Canadian economy and, also, to supply fishermen with information relating to new developments and new techniques introduced through research by the fisheries research board. These researches are of great value to our fishermen and to the fishing industry as a whole.
Closely related to this information and educational service is the consumer branch of the special services of the department. We all approve the work that is being done by this branch of the department. Considerable work has been done in the test kitchens here in Ottawa. Recipe booklets have been distributed throughout the country; home economists and dieticians have been stationed at various points; pamphlets have been distributed, and advertising has been done through radio, television, newspapers and magazines. This work is very important because our fishing industry must not rely

Supply-Fisheries
entirely on its export market. Good advertising, a better product, better quality and attractive packaging are required if we are to increase our home consumption.
The minister mentioned in the course of his remarks that the domestic consumption of fish showed an upward trend but I would ask that more effort be directed toward increasing the consumption of fish in Canada. In 1948, Canadians were consuming between 11 and 12 pounds of fish per person. Ten years later, in 1958, notwithstanding the hard work which had been done by the department, consumption had increased to only 13J pounds. Let us try to realize, Mr. Chairman, what it would mean if this increase could go up to, say, 15 or 16 pounds. It would mean that an additional 40 to 50 million pounds of fish would be consumed yearly in our country. In Japan, for instance, the consumption of fish is a high as 65 or 70 pounds per person per year.
I should also like to say a few words about the 12 mile limit and the privileges granted to foreign trawlers which may come as close as three miles to our shores. I remember the attitude taken by certain members of this house now sitting on the government side, and I recall the remarks which were made by the present Minister of National Revenue and others. The Prime Minister, addressing a meeting in Yarmouth said, as I mentioned a few moments ago, that his government was taking the first firm stand toward protecting our Canadian fishermen. We all know that the meeting which was held last year in Geneva was organized not by the present government but by the previous administration and that it was announced in this house almost two years ago by the former minister of fisheries, the Hon. James Sinclair. We regret that no favourable or final decision has been reached at that conference.
Speaking about the rights of our fishermen I should like once again to bring to the attention of the minister the situation of our small fishermen, inshore fishermen particularly, in the bay of Chaleur area on both sides of the bay, on the Gaspe coast and on the New Brunswick side, where fishermen operating with small boats and using trawls are being interfered with by dragger operations. I would suggest to the minister that a conference be called between the federal government and officials of the provincial governments of New Brunswick and Quebec to discuss this important situation. This is a matter which has been brought to the attention of the department on many occasions and I would suggest again that a line be drawn from Maisonnette on the New Brunswick side to Paspebiac on the Quebec side, and that no draggers be allowed to fish inside of that line until at least November 1 of
[Mr. Robichaud.l
each year. This would give a chance to fishermen operating in small boats and using trawls to save their equipment and their nets.
I mentioned earlier that good work was done by the department in protection services, and one of the main fisheries which requires great activity by the department in this respect is the lobster fishery. I now ask the minister if any further consideration has been given to the suggestion which was made by certain members of the standing committee on fisheries that the department follow the example of the state of Maine in purchasing from the fishermen berried lobsters, that is female lobsters bearing eggs. In this connection I am sure the department will realize that bearing in mind our thousands of miles of shore and the fact that there are probably over 20,000 lobster fishermen, such a system would be impracticable and almost impossible to operate.
I would also ask the minister to give serious consideration, if he has not already done so, to the hour of opening of the lobster season. The present regulations provide that no fisherman shall leave for the fishing ground with lobster traps or gear before 12 noon on the day preceding the opening of the lobster fishing season. In some districts, including Westmorland, Kent county and parts of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, permission was given this year to the fishermen to leave for the fishing grounds two hours earlier. I suggest that this present regulation is unfair to certain fishermen. We have areas where there are no landing facilities available and where fishermen can only sail at high tide. In other areas there are small wharves which can only be used at high tide. And so, the fishermen in adjoining fishing communities have the advantage of being able to get to the fishing grounds hours before those to whom these facilities have not been provided. I suggest to the minister that a change be made and that lobster fishermen be given permission to leave for the fishing grounds at
9.00	a.m. of the day preceding the opening of the fishing season.
Another matter that is of concern to vessel owners on the Atlantic coast is the provision made for subsidies on certain types of long liners or draggers. During world war II, in order to increase the production of food, a subsidy program was introduced as an endeavour to modernize the east coast fishing fleet. Following the war period this subsidy program was further extended to modernize the methods of fishing especially for ground fish and to make it possible for individual fishermen or groups of fishermen to acquire larger and more efficient vessels, and to produce fish at a cost competitive

with other countries fishing on the Atlantic coast area. This program has now reached the point where substantial changes should be made in order to meet new requirements and additional costs of construction.
In 1946, for example, a 55 to 60-foot drag-ger could be built in New Brunswick for $23,000; in 1953, $39,000; in 1955, $46,000; and in 1957, although the vessels were four or five feet longer they cost $53,000 in New Brunswick and as much as $65,000 in Nova Scotia.
From 1946 to 1948, a subsidy of $165 per gross ton amounted to 25 per cent of the cost of a dragger. In 1955 it covered only 18 per cent and in 1957 it represented only 14 per cent or 15 per cent of the total cost. I realize that my time has expired, Mr. Chairman, but I could finish in three or four minutes if I had the unanimous consent of the committee.

The figures I have given refer to New Brunswick. In Nova Scotia in 1957 the subsidy represented only between 10 and 12 per cent of the cost of the boat. As those figures will show, the cost of building a dragger equipped with modern facilities has practically doubled in the last ten or 12 years. If this program is to meet the present requirements and if it is to serve the purpose for which it was introduced it should be increased from $165 to $265 per gross ton and this at very little additional cost to the federal treasury. I urge the minister to give serious consideration to this request.
The members of the committee on marine and fisheries were pleased to hear from Dr. Kask, chairman of the fisheries research board, that a great deal of information had been developed on the use of the so-called waste or by-products from the fishery. We all recognize the high natural vitamin potency which is contained in the liver of certain types of fish such as cod. Dr. Kask informed the committee that the scientists had found what they called a liver residue or special food in these cod livers. They have also found an accessory food element in the residue which can add to the speedy growth of cattle and chickens, thus giving an additional food value to such livers. We understand that in order to be practical and economical, sufficient supply of raw material is required for such production. In most fishing districts processing plants are scattered over long areas of coastlines and 57071-3-247J
Supply-Fisheries
although the amount of waste material is quite substantial, it is in most cases rather difficult to transport and accumulate it in a central area without adding further cost to the raw material.
We all know that animal protein comprises today a big food requirement throughout the world, and while such protein has been developed on an experimental scale by the fisheries research board, further economic studies are required to ascertain if it can be made up in sufficient quantities in order that the large food firms could rely on a continuing source of supply.
We have in my constituency of Gloucester one of the largest concentrations of landings of fresh cod and related species on the Atlantic coast, a fact I drew to the attention of the committee on marine and fisheries. The 60 to 70 draggers operating during a period of five months land at three different landing points within a distance of 20 miles during that period from 50 to 60 million pounds of fresh fish. The quantity of waste from these fresh fish is one of the largest in any area on the Atlantic coast. This area would be an ideal location for a pilot plant to take care of waste products and I urge the minister and his officials to give serious consideration to such an establishment in Gloucester county.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would urge the minister to have his department conduct more research which is needed if some sectors of the fishing industry and particularly the salt fish industry are to continue to exist. Such research is too costly to be undertaken by the industry alone and it requires cooperation from the government. As I have said, this co-operation is essential to the maintenance of the fishing industry.
At this time we must seriously examine what is going on in the United States. I wish to quote at this point, and these will be my last words, a portion of an article entitled "Now Our Fisheries Are Threatened" which appeared in the Financial Post of July 26, 1958:
There is fresh trouble brewing for the Canadian fishing industry which is the mainstay of about 96,000 Canadians. Our catch is worth around $200 million a year.
The Americans, having been thoroughly debauched by elaborate schemes for artificial aid to the American farmers (mainly the rich ones, as it turns out) may now be going in for similar schemes to aid their commercial fishermen.
A bill for this purpose is now in congress and has strong support, not just because the fishermen want to get in on the great Washington giveaways, but because they have been angered and frustrated by two Eisenhower vetoes on their schemes to impose import restrictions.
The plan is dangerous for Canada-and not only because it would spread the handout poison and tend to encourage other pressure groups to stage their own raid on the public treasury.

Supply-Fisheries
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister to give extremely earnest consideration to taking measures to assist the Canadian fishing industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should be very remiss if I did not at this time address the committee on the estimates which are now under study. The fishing industry is the one and only industry in my riding and as such 100 per cent of its population depend on this industry as a means of survival. The sea has always been the alma nutrix of life and its fish produce plays a very substantial part in the economy of Canada.
I should like to take a few minutes in which to pay tribute to the fishermen of this country whom I regard as the hardiest, most fearless and most persistent of workers. They are the hardiest because they know of no limit to the hours they put into the pursuit of their trade. I suggest they are the most fearless because nature with all its whims and fancies does not deter them from pursuing their occupation. They are rocked and rolled not to the music of a Presley or an Anka but by the fury of the sea and wind. Now rising heavenwards, now diving to the depths, they courageously persist in a trade which has not given them a fair return for their labour. Their courage equals that of a Cartier, a Champlain or a Raleigh.
I was glad to note in the speech from the throne that agriculture would be assisted to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and rightly so. In fact, I have searched for arguments in favour of aid to agriculture which would not apply to fisheries and I must admit that I cannot differentiate the need of the one from the other so far as the cod fisherman is concerned.
The general problem is definitely one of cost of production and a low return for their produce but I am pleased to note that after a request was made by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, the hon. member for Gas-pe and the hon. member for Gloucester during the last session for an investigation into price spreads, being the difference between the price paid to the producer and that paid by the consumer, the government has taken action and is now having a study made of the problem.
The major problem, however, seems to be concentrated on the Magdalen islands where the catch of cod has fallen off very seriously and the possibility of an economic crisis exists. Although these hardy people slave at their occupation they are not catching any quantity of cod. As a result, their income is limited and they are not benefiting from the

credits of unemployment insurance stamps and will not receive any benefits during the coming winter.
I can see no alternative to this problem except, as in the case of agriculture, that a method of making deficiency payments be set up to alleviate circumstances such as these. I admit that many problems will be encountered in trying to institute such a policy but I feel confident that the present government, which is so concerned about the people in low income brackets, will find a formula suitable to the cod fishermen of the Magdalen islands, the Gaspe coast and the whole eastern seaboard.
I also wish to commend the spirit of cooperation which exists between the Department of Fisheries and the department of fisheries of the province of Quebec and their recent combined effort which resulted in locating herring to be used as bait in the vicinity of the Magdalen islands.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to extend to the Minister of Fisheries and his officials my sincere congratulations and thanks for their co-operation in assisting me whenever I require their services. The organization of the Newfoundland fishing industry has deep, historical roots. This industry developed during the period from 1750 to 1900, its mainstay or principal product from the beginning being the production of dry salted fish for export.
The market for the product of the industry has been the Mediterranean and Caribbean countries, low income areas of primary production also and subject to periodic business depressions. Because of the absence of alternative employment in Newfoundland the effects of such depressions have generally been borne by the fishermen. Since the 1870's the principal instruments of production have been the cod trap, the hook and line and trawls utilizing the inshore runs of codfish in early summer and fall. Settlement has been determined largely by the location of trap berths and adjacent offshore fishing locations along the coast. At the present time there are about
15.000	fishermen in Newfoundland and about
1.000	fishing settlements scattered over some
6.000	miles of coastline. Most of these fishermen are still dependent on the traditional industry.
I feel that at this time I am forced to speak about a campaign promise to provide floor prices for Newfoundland fishery products. This promise was said to have been made by no less a personage than the Prime Minister. It was widely circulated in my riding as well as elsewhere in Newfoundland and became a catch-cry for many candidates. Floor prices for fish, it was claimed, would be one

of the first acts of the new Progressive Conservative administration. I had expected a reference to this matter in the speech from the throne and I am still waiting. Another season of activity has just about ended. Floor prices for fish made a good election promise but as of now there is nothing to show that the plan will ever be anything but a promise.
It is not my intention to take up the time of the committee with the recounting of such incidents as can be drawn from Newfoundland's experience with the present administration. When I speak to this house about the need of a floor price for fishery products it may sound to most of you like just one more demand from one more region of Canada. Perhaps, however, you will tend to be more sympathetic to the over-all problem of the Newfoundland fishery when I tell you that in this modern era there are still fishermen in Newfoundland, many of them in my riding, who make from their calling substantially less than $1,000 a year. Often they are not fortunate enough to find alternative employment in the off-season and this year is no exception because with the apparent recession we are going through in the newsprint industry work is not going to be very easily found.
Some of the great centres of the Newfoundland fishery are to be found along the coast of my riding, and the marks of a proud history are visible to this day in the character and personality of the fine people whom I am honoured to represent. In my riding of Trinity-Conception ancient fish drying flakes exist in the very shadow of modern fish processing plants, providing a near perfect example of the ancient and the modern that is Newfoundland today. Sleek new draggers steam past the cockleshell punts and skiffs of the inshore fishermen, at places like Bay de Verde, Port-de-Grave, Little Catalina and Southport, but always the calling is the same, to reap the incredible harvest of an enormously bountiful ocean, for in more than 450 years one thing has not changed-Newfoundland's waters continue to abound with fish in a hundred varieties.
Here is a challenge to federal planners. In a hungry world, surely methods can be found to convert this teeming natural wealth into food for the undernourished millions and into a way of life for Newfoundlanders that comes reasonably close to the concept of confederation that all of us share. We hear a great deal about the untapped resources Canada possesses. Those who make such statements are referring to minerals, water power or timber. But, Mr. Chairman, it is not at all inconceivable, in fact it is quite probable that the wealth to be found in the waters of
Supply-Fisheries
Newfoundland may well turn out to be of even greater value than some of the other more readily recognized resources of a growing nation. I should like to see this government embark on a program of exploration of the great fisheries of Canada, and to pursue that avenue of development. I hope most sincerely that the fisheries will not be forgotten or relegated to a back seat in the overall planning of Canada's big and more rewarding tomorrow.
In view of the announcement of the withdrawal of the exclusive right of export of the salt cod by the Newfoundland Fish Exporters Limited, it is hoped, and I urgently impress this upon the responsible ministers, that measures will be taken with the least possible delay to set up an improved system to protect the marketing of salt codfish in the best interests of the Newfoundland fisherman and the industry generally.
The shortage of bait in Newfoundland is so serious that at this time the Department of Fisheries has arranged for a supply from the maritimes. I refer you to page 3505 of Hansard for August 14, 1958 where I asked the Minister of Fisheries if his department had taken steps to relieve the shortage, and the minister replied as follows:
This is something of which my department is very much aware, and the difficulty arises because of the failure of the squid fishery this year. I might say that during last winter the department's bait service froze more herring bait than ever before, but these stocks are now almost exhausted and a fairly critical situation has arisen.
The department, however, has embarked on a serious attempt to relieve the situation. For example, we have two helicopters under charter to the department scouting for squid. I am happy to say that a certain amount of squid has just now been obtained about 30,000 pounds, and it will be delivered very shortly to the areas where it is most urgently needed. We hope to augment this supply. In addition we have obtained 150,000 pounds of herring in the Yarmouth area, which will be delivered to the bait depots in Newfoundland as quickly as we can get suitable transports-tion for it.
I should like to commend the Minister of Fisheries for this action, although at the same time I should like to impress upon him that steps should be taken to ensure that in the future the Newfoundland bait depots will be always fully stocked with emergency supplies to guard against a possible shortage. It must be stressed that any shortage such as that experienced at the present time means a severe loss of much needed employment to our hard-working fishermen. As a matter of fact, the bait situation was so serious that the minister temporarily suspended the sale of bait to foreign fishing vessels. Again, I am glad that our fishermen got priority, but of course this is as it should be.

Supply-Fisheries
It is very encouraging to know that the Department of Fisheries has developed a small mobile refrigerated holding unit which should be of untold value in serving the many fishing communities throughout Newfoundland. Even though this will not prove to be a cure-all, it is sincerely hoped that it will go a long way towards meeting the bait servicing problems. I should like once more to commend the minister and his officials for this realistic approach to a very important problem.
The former administration, as well as the provincial government of Newfoundland, put a great deal of thought and effort into the artificial drying of salted codfish, and it is good to know that the present administration is actively continuing this important work. It is hoped that continued study will prove beneficial to our fishermen, as I am convinced it will.
As the committee is aware, the former administration saw fit to subsidize the price of salt, a commodity which is vital to our salt cod industry. This measure has proven to be very helpful, and I would urge the present administration to not only continue this helpful form of assistance but improve upon it if possible.
I mentioned earlier the serious shortage of bait in Newfoundland. This applies to squid, herring and caplin. I understand the shortage of squid because I am led to believe that they have not appeared in Newfoundland waters this year in the usual large numbers. Of course, this does not explain why the caplin were not frozen and stored, because these small fish appeared in Newfoundland waters in tremendous quantities this year. In so far as herring are concerned, there has been great concern throughout Newfoundland for many years because of their failure to appear in large schools as they have in the past. Surely, in such an important branch of the fishing industry as herring, as well as squid, the fishery research board should put a great deal of effort into research work and exploratory fishing in an attempt to find the cause of the failure of these fish to appear or to locate the schools wherever they may be.
Newfoundland's fisheries rank among the richest and most important in the world, and many Newfoundlanders, directly or indirectly, gain their livelihood from fisheries or trades allied thereto. Many fishing craft of all sorts and sizes are engaged in the shore and bank fishery. Salted codfish is not an unwanted article of food. As a matter of fact, world consumption has increased and the departments of fisheries and trade and commerce

must see that we maintain our present markets as well as obtain new ones, and make sure that our fishermen get a proper return for their efforts.
Our fresh fish industry has witnessed a remarkable development. In 1938, we exported approximately 500,000 pounds of fresh fish and in 1957 we exported approximately 53 million pounds. A great deal of the byproducts of this industry have been utilized as offal. We hope to see our fresh fish industry continue to grow and expand and to maintain its high standard in the export field.
