speechtext:
I would like to join other members who have spoken in this debate in expressing appreciation for the helpfulness and the general attitude shown by the minister and his officials when they appeared before the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I am sure this committee gave some of us an opportunity to learn more of the details of the complexities in the fisheries industries of our country and to better assess the effect of the actions of the department on fisheries in all parts of Canada, not from a provincial or parochial point of view but from the point of view of the effect upon Canada as a whole. I have but one or two comments to make at this time and one or two questions to pose because I think the bulk of the work was done in committee, undoubtedly in a very excellent way. The answers given were complete and detailed.
The population of Canada, as in many other nations, is slowly increasing in size, and history has shown that generally speaking when countries increase their population beyond

a certain point there is a greater tendency to use the products of the sea as foodstuffs. Some nations do so perhaps because of a decline in the richness of the arable land and others because their arable land may be insufficient to provide the per capita requirements of food. They consequently look to the sea for a supplement to their diets. We know that fish is a high quality and high protein food. I personally am more partial to fish than to other protein foods, although this partiality may not be shared by many people. In the years to come I am sure, however, that we in Canada will be in the same position as that of other countries in the past, having to look to the ocean for additional foodstuffs, not only for domestic use but also for use as exports to other nations.
We must make sure that our present fisheries are maintained and must also enhance them and attempt to guarantee that other industries and interests do not enter in a detrimental way into the fisheries of our nation. I am thinking particularly of the hydroelectric interests in so far as the province of British Columbia is concerned, where we have had a fish versus power controversy for some time. So far as I know, not too much damage has been done to the fisheries as yet, but there is a possibility that in the future, if the power interests are allowed to have their way and are given the right to develop fish rivers for hydroelectric purposes, this will have a detrimental effect upon the fisheries of British Columbia, particularly the salmon fisheries. I know that the attitude of the minister and his departmental officials as expressed in the standing committee is one which will ensure to the greatest possible extent that our fish rivers are protected and that our migrating fish, particularly the salmon, are not interfered with by the development of these rivers for hydroelectric purposes.
We must do everything we possibly can to ensure that none of our fish rivers is harmfully developed for hydroelectric purposes although our power requirements are met. Within the next decade or thereabouts we will in fact probably have protected our present fish rivers and to the greatest possible degree will have met the demands for power for it is to be hoped that by that time sufficient research and engineering work will have been done with respect to nuclear energy that we may channel nuclear power into the generation of electric power.

We have in British Columbia very large potential hydroelectric sites which in no way will affect the fisheries of the Pacific coast. I refer particularly to the Columbia river also to the so-called Wenner-Gren project in the northern part of the province, and I hope the department will be able to maintain the position it has held over the years of protecting our fish rivers, and also that other parts of government, the federal government and the provincial government in British Columbia, will be able to co-operate in such a way that these potential hydroelectric sites may be developed so that the fullest possible service can be given to the general public. I am sure that if we operate in that light we will be meeting the hydroelectric requirements and doing so in such a way as to guarantee that the operation of these sites and the distribution of electrical power will serve the interest of the public to the greatest possible extent. We will also be laying the ground work for the possibility of using nuclear power in the years to come, and we will have the best of both worlds, as it were, arising out of that sort of action.
I should like to mention also to the minister a matter which comes under the Department of Agriculture. If it has not already been drawn to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries, if he would look at Hansard for August 1, beginning on page 2964 he would find on that page and on a number of pages following a discussion between the Minister of Agriculture and myself with respect to the granting of subsidies under the Cold Storage Act. I think that a few months ago the policy of the government was that they would make a grant of one-third of the cost toward building public cold storage facilities. Recently, the regulations have changed so that a maximum of $50,000 was placed on this one-third of the total cost, and the information we were able to get from the Minister of Agriculture in this regard, very briefly, was that the reason behind the imposition of this $50,000 limit was, apparently, that there were sufficient cold storage facilities in some areas as not to warrant additional subsidies on the part of the government and that these cold storage facilities were, in the main being used only to the extent of 50 per cent of their capacity. If the minister would read Hansard of August 1 he would be able to get a far more complete picture than I am able to give at this time and one which can only be obtained after reading all the questions and answers as they developed.
I directed some questions to the Minister of Agriculture on that occasion, asking if
Supply-Fisheries
he could give me some statistical information about the number of cold storage facilities which handled fish products, the number which handled agricultural products and the number which handled foodstuffs of a mixed nature, but the minister did not have those facts available in detail on that occasion. Subsequently he sent me a letter and I should like to draw it to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries. It amplifies the information which was given me on August 1 and it says, in part:
My department informs me that there are 249 warehouses in Canada which store exclusively, or in the main, fish or fisheries products and 1,969 which store in the main agricultural products and, in addition, 849 warehouses which are classified as general, i.e. storing a variety of products.
The view we think should be taken with regard to the operation of the Cold Storage Act is this: there are approximately, as shown in this letter, eight times as many agricultural products cold storage warehouses as there are fisheries products cold storage warehouses, and I think it would be more advantageous to meeting the need that exists at least in some parts of the country-and in one case with which I am particularly concerned-if we could divide the consideration of the application of this subsidy as between fisheries products cold storage needs and agricultural products cold storage needs. If we do that I am sure the fishery requirements would not then be affected by the conditions which exist in the agricultural products field.
I hope the minister will undertake to consult with the Minister of Agriculture from the point of view of attempting to consider separately the requirements of fish cold storage facilities as opposed to agricultural cold storage facilities. If the minister does that and has, correspondingly, more say in the granting of such subsidies I am sure we will be able to reverse the decision of the Department of Agriculture which, I think, is not justified as it applies to fish cold storage facilities, and revert to the provision which existed previously, namely a one-third subsidy having a $50,000 limit.
I have one or two other questions to ask, and it may well be I could pose them now since I have a few minutes left before six o'clock. Perhaps the minister could get additional information, if it is required, during the supper hour and answer them at eight o'clock.
One relates to a specific vote concerning the operation of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission. I understand there is a meeting, which may still be in progress, of a committee of the Pacific salmon fisheries commission which is being held in

Supply-Fisheries
Hawaii. I wonder whether the minister is able to impart to this committee any information as to the conclusions or recommendations which have been made arising out of the meeting in Hawaii of this tripartite committee.
In addition, I again wish to raise the question of the conflict which exists with respect to this research work which is being done in the north Pacific about salmon-who gets them, where they intermingle and so on. There has been quite a bit of controversy over this in years past, and in this regard I directed a question to the minister on May 21, and the answer which he gave, if I may quote it in part, was this:
The Canadian part of the co-ordinated research program in 1958 consists of having two large vessels make two cruises each, one in March and one in August, north of latitude 45 degrees north just east of longitude 175 degrees west.
I wonder if the minister is in a position to indicate what information this cruise that was made in March has produced, or whether it is more desirous to wait until the research program of August is completed and until the spot fishing tests which were to be made from mid-May to mid-September are completed so we will have a complete look at the information those vessels are able to procure.
The attitude of the department with respect to previous research trips into the north Pacific area based on the data they were able to compile was that no Canadian fish had been caught by Japanese fisheries in that area. There are two reasons for the conflict concerning whether or not Japanese fisheries are catching Canadian fish in the high seas in the mid-Pacific and one reason is this. In the past Canadian research vessels did not travel beyond the 155th degree of west longitude which is 20 degrees of longitude or roughly 750 miles west of this line. The other reason is that we in Canada have relied upon information collected by United States research vessels that were supposed to have been in the area between 155 degrees west and 175 degrees west. The contention is that by relying on the information collected by the United States vessels we did not have an opportunity to see in full detail the statistical information that was compiled but rather we relied only on the interpretation placed on that information by the United States officials involved. Also, the studies of the United States research vessels were primarily directed toward gathering evidence for the protection of the Bristol Bay sockeye and other Alaska salmon and not toward gathering information with respect to our own Canadian salmon.

The Alaska Sportsman of April 1958 carried an interesting article on this question. Whether or not the conclusions drawn in the article are based on scientific studies is beyond my knowledge but the fact is that publicity has been given by an Alaskan magazine to the question of research conducted in the north Pacific. The article states in part:
-American salmon mingle with salmon of Asiatic origin. At 175 degrees west longitude, stocks are 90 per cent American and 10 per cent Asian. Even at 170 degrees east the ratio is 40 per cent American and 60 per cent Asiatic salmon.
The article then goes on to make reference to catches and other matters but the point is that the United States research vessels as indicated in this article have conducted their research with relation to American or Alaskan salmon and not to Canadian salmon as indicated by the references to the ratio of the catch.
I have not seen all the statistical information gathered by Canadian, United States and Japanese research vessels and indeed even if I had I would not be able to interpret it or know precisely what it means. But there is this difference of opinion as to whether or not the Japanese are catching our salmon on the high seas. For that reason I was interested to learn what the minister said on May 21 to the effect that our research vessels this year are to move out in the area up to 175 degrees where we had not ventured before. I hope as a result of this move and the information collected from the studies made we will be able to state as a definite scientific fact whether or not the Japanese are catching our salmon or, as a result of that, we will be able to agree with the members of the tripartite commission that a certain non-fishing area should be declared there. I believe it is a proven fact that to catch salmon on the high seas means catching them before they are fully grown. In effect this does not allow the salmon to mature and has a detrimental effect on our entire fisheries interests.
In making these remarks I had to digress to a certain degree and deal with a matter that perhaps more properly could have been dealt with when the specific vote is called but I thought it necessary to include that topic in my general remarks. I hope the minister will be able to deal with the questions I raised when he rises to reply on this vote but if he desires to hold over some aspects of the questions and answer them on specific votes that will be perfectly satisfactory.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the fishery is the oldest industry in Canada and probably ever since there was a fishery there have been problems connected with it. But no one can say the fisheries did not get off to a good start. When John Cabot discovered the new world he made his voyage of discovery looking for gold, silver and precious stones. Instead he found codfish but over the years the fisheries he discovered have brought in more wealth than his backers could have ever hoped to find in the form of gold mines or diamonds. But since its inception this ancient industry has run into peculiar and serious problems from time to time. These problems are not peculiar to modern times alone. A great Canadian statesman revered by all, perhaps particularly so by a large section of this house, and who at one time, I believe, occupied the offices now occupied by the Minister of Fisheries, Sir John A. Macdonald, had this to say in writing on May 1, 1878 to Sir Stafford North-cote with respect to confederation with Newfoundland:
Lastly, it is of importance to imperial interests that Newfoundland should be added to the dominion. It would complete the great scheme of British North American confederation begun in 1867-it would relieve the colonial office from the trouble and responsibility of the direct government of the island, and it would throw upon Canada the burthen of its defence. And that defence would necessitate the creation of something like a naval force by our government. But more than all, in any future negotiations with the United States on the troublesome question of the fisheries, the subject could be dealt with as a whole.
Later in 1890 he again referred to the fisheries when he said with respect to Newfoundland and the Dominion of Canada:
At present the policies of the two governments on commercial, fishing and other questions are often divergent.
I think that even today the problems which Newfoundland has and those of the rest of Canada are sometimes divergent. But it is not for want of constant reminder that we have not yet solved the problems of the fisheries of the east coast. I would be the last one to say that nothing has been done because a great deal has been done to improve the fisheries in my native province. The provincial government, with its policy of assisting industry, has helped to bring about what may well be described as a revolution in the fisheries, particularly in its assistance in the industrialization of the fisheries; while on the other hand the impact of confederation on Newfoundland was perhaps nowhere more marked than in the fishing industry because the government of Canada, through
Supply-Fisheries
its Department of Fisheries, has been giving excellent service to the province of Newfoundland.
But the whole problem, although bit by bit it is being attended to, has never been completely solved nor has a way yet been found to place the fisheries upon the same basis as the other great industries of Canada. The fisheries of this country are without doubt one of our great national resources. We talk of spending huge sums of money on the development of various parts of our great nation but I do not think that relatively we are spending either enough effort or enough money on the development of our fisheries. I might use a scriptural phrase in describing all the laudable attempts being made to develop and exploit our industries and resources-"these ought ye to have done but not to have left the other undone".
It is no longer a secret that the ships of at least 10 nations are fishing off our shores. While those concerned with the defence of the country are somewhat worried over the presence of large trawlers in our waters, I do not think that comparable worry is evinced over the trade which fishing fleets of foreign nations are taking away from us. Instead of being the foremost fishing country in the world we are being pushed back from that position and we shall soon lose our lead completely.
For years I have heard scientists and economists tell us that the greatest fishery ever known, the trap fishery of Newfoundland, was doing the fisheries more harm than good. I cannot subscribe to that opinion. It is true that vast quantities of fish come in during the short season and are trapped. They must be caught and processed quickly and it has been difficult to find a way to do that other than by the old methods used since John Cabot discovered Newfoundland. But if the great canning plants of this continent can deal with fruits and vegetables which have short seasons I see no reason why the scientific ingenuity available in this modern age cannot look after the surplus fish that come to Canadian waters during what we call the trap fishery.
Again, while large fleets of ships are in Newfoundland waters comparatively few of them are Canadian ships. We have three large trawlers, the largest being approximately 400 tons. Then we have a total of 50 other trawlers and 13 draggers above 100 tons and five between 75 and 100 tons. Perhaps more than anyone else I am aware of the need to extend help to the small fishermen, the need for small harbours, dredging work, navigational aids, salt assistance and loans
3S04

Supply-Fisheries
to these fishermen, but at the same time I do not think we should overlook the need for a large deep sea fleet.
There appears to be nothing we can do to prevent our competitors from fishing off our shores on the Newfoundland banks but certainly there is something we can do to compete with them by bringing about greater and cheaper production and better markets. While the fresh fish industry is growing and thriving the salt fish industry, which is really the basis of Newfoundland economy, is dwindling. But the salt fish business is still the basic industry of the country. Of a total of 16,000 to 17,000 people in the fisheries about 12,000 are employed in the salt codfish business.
The salt cod fishery is really the foundation of our economy and is a sort of buffer industry which takes up the slack when other employment fails. This is particularly noticeable this year when there has been a falling off of construction work and woods employment and perhaps nearly 2,000 more men have returned to the fishery.
However, the time is going to come when they will not be able to do that. A farmer can become a miner and a miner can become a woods operator, but a deep-sea fisherman has to be bred to the sea. Let the young men who normally prosecute the fisheries get away from them or not go into the fisheries in the first place and it is doubtful if they would be able, even if they were willing, to return to the salt codfish industry or the deep-sea fishery later in life. There are many men, to my own personal knowledge, who would rather be fishermen if they could make the same living as fishermen as they can as mechanics. However, the return from the salt cod fishery is so low that they choose other work, although as a vocation they would much prefer to be fishermen.
One thing that would help the fisheries considerably would be a direct shipping line to the West Indies. Since Newfoundland is an island she cannot exploit the mainland markets and should be given assistance in getting fish to the market at the same cost as her sister Atlantic provinces. Again this year there seems to be a shortage of bait and a shortage of salt and both of these factors adversely affect codfishing. Then, too, we have to compete with subsidies. For instance, the Icelandic government subsidizes its fishermen sometimes paying as much as $360 per fishing boat per day. The French subsidize their fishermen. I believe the Portuguese government pays a subsidy as well. It is true that Portugal does not compete with us in foreign markets. At one time, Portugal was a market for our fish, but as she produced more and more herself we could not sell any

more there. The payment of these subsidies makes it extremely difficult for Canadian fishermen to make a living and still sell their fish cheaply enough to compete with these other nations.
All in all, the present position is that there seems to be a steady decline in the amount of salt codfish produced. I am not sure that the contention that we produce a product expensively to sell to poor markets is altogether true. Where is there stronger buying power, except in the United States, than in Puerto Rico, Cuba, Jamaica, Brazil and such countries?
A few minutes ago I mentioned that there were the fleets of ten nations operating on the grand banks. I, myself, have seen fleets of white-painted ships standing out of the harbour of St. John's in all their magnificence, but they were not Canadian ships. I have seen throngs of fishermen on the streets of St. John's, but they were not Canadian nationals. The fruits of the sea which these sailors were harvesting represent a loss of trade to us. Earlier I referred to the fact that Iceland subsidizes its fishermen. It is interesting to note that Newfoundland lost the Jamaican market to Iceland recently. It is interesting also to note that yesterday it was announced that Russia is lending Iceland $3.5 million for the construction of fishing boats. It is worth noting that the Canadian trade with Jamaica is as much as 2| to 3 times in our favour, and that sugar from the West Indies is coming in under a protective tariff which will possibly put the New Brunswick refineries out of business. I rather think that is turning the other cheek a little bit too often.
The removal of the exclusive right of NAFEL to export fish is something which I should like the Department of Fisheries to consider very carefully. It is true that there should be free trade between our own provinces, but I should like to point out that the fish produced in Newfoundland is produced by virtue of the plants that already exist there, the stores, the wharves and so on, all of which cost a lot of money and represent capital invested in Newfoundland by the local fish trade. If the product which that investment makes possible is to be processed by a sister province which has no risk capital involved, it places the whole structure of the local industry in jeopardy.
The oldest industry in Canada, Mr. Chairman, can I am sure become even at this late date a profitable one. We pride ourselves on the size of our nation. We are proud of the fact that it extends from sea to sea. We are proud of the motto that the wholesome sea is at the eastern and western gates of Canada. But if we confine our efforts to the

exploitation of the land and stop at the seashore, there is really little reason for us to take pride in the rolling billows. The proper development and exploitation of our great and wealthy country should not stop at the seashore but should extend into the waters which surround us, waters which are ours, waters which have in them the wealth which for hundreds of years has provided a livelihood for many of our best citizens and supplied Canada with an export trade of great value.
Certainly, it is to the interest of all to develop the whole of Canada, including the wealth that is in the sea. With the capacities we have today, natural and acquired, with our native ingenuity, scientific skill and commercial force, we can inject into this ancient industry the virility which is the hallmark of Canadian enterprise.

-representing Queens-Lunenberg and living in the town of Lunenberg, the home of the largest deep-sea fishing fleet in North America, I feel it is only proper that I should make a few remarks on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries.
First, I should like to congratulate the minister on the high honour that was bestowed upon him by Mount Allison University last Saturday. I shall try to make my remarks as brief as possible, but there are a few points that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Many of my constituents are directly concerned with the fishing industry and any changes that affect this industry have a direct bearing on their earnings.
In recent years there has been a gradual change taking place within the fishing industry and this change is quite evident when you travel the south shore of Nova Scotia. You will see along the coast small wharves and fish sheds, and long rows of fish flakes which are deteriorating In the sun. Formerly fish were landed at these small wharves and were washed there by the fishermen and their wives. But today as we have progressed in the industry, modern fish dryers have been installed in the larger plants, and also automatic fish washing machines, thus eliminating the need for the old fashioned method of drying fish in the sun. However, there are many who will argue that sun dried fish are of higher quality; and as a matter of interest I may say that the Gaspe cure does have a preference in certain markets
Supply-Fisheries
throughout the world. However, those within the industry are today mostly concerned with the marketing and catching of fish.
For the benefit of those who are not familiar with the fishing industry I should like to point out that it is divided into two sections. There is the salt fishing industry and there is the fresh fishing industry. Of late, we have heard a good deal about the salt fishing industry owing to the loss of one of its most important markets in Jamaica. The control of fish imports in this British West Indies island rests with trade minister the Hon. Wills O. Isaacs. We have recently seen this island of Jamaica buying some 3,000 tons of salt cod from Iceland on the grounds that the price is about one half cent a pound below that quoted by the Canadian trade.
Trade should be a two-way street. We buy a good deal of sugar from the island of Jamaica. In fact, in 1956 Canadian refineries bought 36 per cent of Jamaica's 1956 sugar production or 132,000 tons. If this sugar had been bought from a non-commonwealth producing country the Canadian treasury would have collected additional import duties of approximately $2,900,000. In that same year the total value of all the salt and pickled fish that Canada sold to Jamaica was approximately $3,255,000. In other words, by virtue of this sugar preference the Jamaican sugar industry obtained from Canadian refineries between $2J million and $3 million more for the sugar sold to Canada in 1956 than would have been realized if this $1 per one hundred pounds preference did not exist. To reduce this situation to a point of being ridiculous, may I say that the Canadian government would have lost out financially only to the extent of $355,000 if we had donated all the salt and pickled fish that Jamaica purchased from Canada in 1956 instead of giving the sugar preference.
In spite of these facts, and in spite of a public statement by the Jamaican minister Mr. Isaacs that the Canadian sugar market is vital to Jamaica's existence, no consideration was given this country by Jamaica when purchasing this 3,000 tons of dried salt codfish. I believe the time has arrived for the Canadian government to speak plainly to the Jamaican government. I do not feel that it would be at all unreasonable to point out to Jamaica that if they want to continue to enjoy the Canadian sugar preference along with tariff preferences on liquor, et cetera, they must decontrol the price of salt cod and let supply, demand and competition prevail. Only in this way can our Canadian salt fish exporters be given the assistance in marketing their product which is so urgently required by this basic industry.

Supply-Fisheries
Assistance to our fresh fish industry is also required. This assistance should take into consideration the increased cost of boats and equipment today as compared with costs say ten years ago. At the present time fishermen receive practically the same prices for their catch as they received ten years ago, this despite the fact that it takes $2 today to purchase what $1 would buy in 1947. The effect of all the scientific advances with regard to refrigeration of fish and improved marketing facilities which have increased sales of this product have not brought an increase of one per cent pound to the fishermen themselves in the last ten years.
The reason that this condition exists is sometimes attributed to larger catches by more mechanized boats, but the truth of the matter is that, regardless of catches, or rates of United States exchange, or shortage of fish, there is no improvement in price to the fishermen. Dominion bureau of statistics figures show a drastic drop in the stocks of fresh and frozen fish in reserve. There is a terrific shortage of ground fish on the banks-I refer to certain types of ground fish such as cod and haddock-and the new regulations with regard to mesh size imposes further hardship on our east coast fishermen who must catch fish each trip to sea or starve. They have no big reserve of capital built up when prices were high, for prices have never been high for this basic food commodity to the primary producer. They have no guaranteed salary and work only in anticipation of their share of the catch.
It is true that they are living and existing but only by working exhausting hours. In fact, men have been known to stand on the deck of a ship dressing fish for some 24 hours at a time, stopping only long enough to eat. They must do this at times in order to clear the deck of fish. But whether the catches are fair or poor, the price remains almost static over the years. This does not apply only to fresh fish but also to the salt fish industry. I believe that some form of assistance must be considered in order to encourage men to continue in this industry.
The department is contemplating further research. I should like to suggest to the minister that further consideration be given to investigating the scallop beds. I have been looking at the new Canadian fishing vessel the A. T. Cameron built for the fisheries research board of Canada. It looks like a very capable ship of a size that will be a credit to Canada and a credit to the men in the department who had a hand in designing this ship. It is a draggers style ship which should certainly be seaworthy.

I should like to suggest that some consideration be given to investigating the scallop beds. This shell-fish now provides a most important source of income to the Atlantic coast fishermen. In fact the 1956 production in the maritime provinces was in excess of $1 million, and production has been growing rapidly. The tremendous improvement in this fishery can be realized when we consider the fact that the catch was valued at less than one-quarter of a million dollars in 1951. The scallop fishery, prior to 1953, was carried out principally by small boats fishing inshore banks close to port. The only exception to this was in the Digby and Northumberland strait area where these fisheries are relatively stable and somewhat larger boats are used, ranging up to 65 feet in length. However, in recent years much larger boats have been used in this fishery, ranging from 90 feet to 95 feet in length, and these boats fish far from their home ports on George's bank close to the coast of the United States and also on the offshore banks of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
It is, however, agreed among these fishermen in my riding that continuous research is necessary in the scallop industry to assist them in locating new beds which, so far as the offshore fishery is concerned, have a tendency to shift with changing water temperatures. I would like to suggest that this information regarding new scallop bed locations be widely advertised by the fisheries department so that all those in the industry may avail themselves of the opportunity to make use of the findings of the department as new beds are discovered. The scallop is highly nutritious and can be conveniently stored, and I would like to suggest that the government further assist this industry by increased advertising and promotion and suggested uses for this fish on Canadian trains and in government institutions.
From information supplied to me by sea captains on the east coast who fish out of my home port of Lunenburg, it is my understanding that stocks of shrimp are on the increase on the offshore banks of Nova Scotia. We are all aware that this shellfish is a delicacy and is what we in the industry call a high priced fish, bringing a return to the fisherman which is comparable to that from lobsters, scallops, halibut and swordfish. In my opinion the fisheries research board should give immediate consideration to investigating the supplies of shrimp which are available in the hope that the quantity of the shrimp on the Nova Scotia cost should be determined and so that the fishermen may be advised whether this fishery could be economically established.

To further greater participation by the fresh fish industry, I would like to suggest that the government increase the present subsidy payment on ships built up to a length of 100 feet. Those who live in the Atlantic provinces realize that in the sea, we have at our front door a great natural resource. This fact is also recognized by France, Portugal, Italy, Spain, the United States and Iceland, to name but a few of the countries and, as the population of the world grows and the amount of arable land diminishes, we must turn to the sea for our food supplies. The encouragement of the construction of draggers up to 100 feet in length would, I believe, be of great importance not only to the fish industry but, having in mind that we no longer have a large merchant fleet, these ships in time of war could be an invaluable asset to the nation.
I would suggest that this government, through the Department of Fisheries, should give serious consideration to extending the present subsidy of $165 per ton, which is limited to ships of up to 65 feet in length, to ships up to 100 feet in length. Further assistance which could be provided to the fresh fishing industry would be the paying of the cost of the ice used by these fishermen. We do assist the salt fish industry at the present time by paying a proportion of the price of the salt used by that industry, and I believe that in keeping with the department's views with respect to having the fish landed in prime condition this assistance could be extended in respect of fresh fish in the manner I have just outlined.
The United States government has, as stated by the hon. member for Gloucester, planned some assistance for their fishing industry, and I believe the time has arrived when consideration must be given to our basic industry in Canada and I hope in this regard that the proposals I have made will be carefully studied for the benefit of the Canadian fishermen.

(Text):
When the first white men came to Nova Scotia it was for one main purpose, to fish. They found that the waters which surrounded the Nova Scotia peninsula were swarming with fish, and year after year they continued to return filling their ships from the bounty of the sea.
Now, four centuries later, fishing is still the main attraction and essential industry, the sole means of livelihood for many, many of my constituents. Fishing is a major and essential industry in my constituency. Therein lies, in my estimation, the Liberal's Waterloo. They were unaware of the necessity for the furtherance of the economy of my constituents. They encouraged them to fish, but neglected to better their lot by providing them with the necessities that are part and parcel of every endeavour. Just drive down from Weymouth, Nova Scotia to the end of Shelburne county and you will be amazed at the scenery, the neat rows of wooden lobster traps, the picturesque Cape Island type boat; but you will also see, in vast numbers, wharves in disrepair, no docking facilities where they should be, inadequate harbour facilities for those who go down to the sea in search of a livelihood. There, in my estimation, lie the relics of Liberal neglect, mute testimonials of their good will, perhaps, but also of their laissez-faire attitude. It is one of the cross-currents that shipwrecked them on the 31st of March.
Already, we of the maritimes are feeling the beneficial effects of the public works program, and I wish to commend the government for its encouraging attitude toward better harbour facilities, a step which, as time goes on, will lengthen its stride, thereby giving the toilers of the deep a means of disposing of their fishery products more quickly and more efficiently, and resulting in better quality.
However, along with the necessity of better harbour and dock facilities to ensure

a high quality of fishery products, I would like, Mr. Chairman, to add a plea that additional transportation means be provided to maintain the renowned high standard of my constituency's lobster and fresh and salt fish, for after this summer we of the town known as the gateway to the maritimes are not assured of the services of the S. S. Yarmouth Castle. In order to fill the breach caused by her departure for other ports, I would urge that the government take under consideration the building of a new ferry to handle the ever-increasing shipments and the mounting tourist trade for, indeed, the latter has increased by leaps and bounds since our friends, the Americans, have become aware of the attractions many and varied offered by this province known as the ocean's playground where one may dip contentedly in the briny deep, and enjoy restful breeze-kissed evenings which ensure peaceful and pleasant slumbers.
Motels and private homes dot the highways where once bushes and alders grew. The national housing loan board, through its ever-increasing expansion and government foresight, makes it possible to meet the growing needs of tourist trade. May I, Mr. Chairman, commend the government for its awareness of the people's problems along this line. We all know that the construction of federal buildings and of private homes means more pay cheques and better trade.
Security for the home-owners and their families naturally springs from the ability of each and every one to earn a decent living wage. However, this does not mean that unemployment-although it is decreasing-does not exist in my riding. It would be foolhardy to deny it. At this moment, nevertheless, I appreciate what the Conservative government has done and is doing to ameliorate the situation, to step in and supplement seasonal lay-offs and lack of work with not only one but two extensions of benefit periods, which in many areas throughout my constituency are a godsend. I know that this is not a cure-all for unemployment ills, but I am sure the hon. members of this committee will agree with me that it is a step in the right direction, and led on by many more steps of this nature, we will, eventually, come to the promised land of peace, prosperity and contentment.
Mr. Chairman, with your kind permission and begging the indulgence of the house, I wish to illustrate the dire need for fishery protection craft, adequately manned and strategically located to assist fishermen in distress. Twenty years ago a near tragedy occurred which forcefully illustrates the lack of adequate search and rescue vessels, and if

hon. members will bear with me, I shall endeavour to substantiate my assertion with a story.
On the 15th of December, 1938, after three days of wintery weather, the sun greeted the village of Pinkney's Point with the promise of a perfect fishing day. The turbulent and angry sea of previous days lazily and reposingly invited the fishermen to venture out and retrieve the lobsters which had crawled into their unmolested traps. As they gladly left the wharf on this eventful morning, no one thought that before another day dawned nerve-wracking tension and heart-rending anxiety would disturb the serenity of this village. For throughout this day, so calm and peaceful, the boats flitted about on the vast expanse, and there the men happily hauled their traps, all the while speculating on the good catch that was theirs. And as the sun slowly sank in the west one by one they returned to the safety of their home port.
However, due to the large quantity of traps, one lagged behind unaware of the impending storm gathering on the horizon, unmindful of the snow that began falling; the men thinking only of the many needed items that their bountiful catch would provide for their beloved ones, thinking, as they worked on, of the rejoicing there would be in their homes that evening as they handed to their wives the day's pay cheque. So absorbed were they that they noticed not the wind's mournful tone and its increasing intensity. Finally the last trap was hauled, and then they compass-pointed the prow of their boat homeward.
However, fate dealt them a cruel hand. The shafting had broken. Hastily, preparations were made to ensure safety while waiting for rescue, but in an hour's time the storm had so intensified that it was impossible for the fleet to venture out. The men of the village remained on the wharf and spoke in hushed tones, knowing that if rescue was not imminent, chances of survival were small. I will not attempt, Mr. Chairman, to describe the gamut of emotions that were part and parcel of that night. The beloved ones lingeringly thought that their morning's kiss would be the last one they would ever have from their beloved husbands.
And on the storm-lashed sea two men fought valiantly for their lives. Their frail craft, tossed about by mountainous seas, happily weathered the storm, and next morning to the rejoicing of all they were towed back to the haven of their home port. The harrowing experience remains indelibly etched on their minds. Thankful that they had been spared, and promise-bound, the next Sunday they came to the village church, garbed in their fishing clothes of black rubber, and as they kneeled at the foot of the altar
Supply-Fisheries
and offered prayers of thanks for having been saved, the congregation also prayed. All eyes bedimmed by tears lifted toward heaven, imploringly pleading for the establishment of rescue service made possible through specially built and crew-manned coast guard vessels.
May I at this point say that in past years many village churches have witnessed such scenes; however, with a slight change in scenery. The congregation and relatives have gathered to pray, yes, but also to mourn and pay their last respects to a loved one lying in a watery grave. For 19 years this plea has fallen on deaf ears and nothing has been done to allay the fears of those who daily pit their skill and daring against the whims of mother nature.
Mr. Chairman, I have endeavoured to present before this committee the wish of every fisherman along the entire sea coast of Nova Scotia. I have also, though perhaps awkwardly, endeavoured to present the wish of every widow and child of those who found a watery grave as their final resting place and on their behalf I respectfully and humbly urge that provision be made for the building of adequate coast guard cutters for the protection of a vast fishing fleet that is part and parcel of Nova Scotia's primary industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is usual to congratulate an hon. member on his maiden speech and I wish to convey my congratulations to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare who has just taken his seat although I must confess I was somewhat concerned when I noticed the huge string of red herrings with which he started out. Once he disposed of these, however, he did very well and I am sure he deserves our congratulations.
These estimates have already been very thoroughly discussed in the standing committee on fisheries and I should like at this time to pay tribute to the hon. member for Gaspe who acted as chairman of that committee, and who conducted the discussions with such great harmony and, I think, with great profit to all of us. I hope that all hon. members will make a point of reading the minutes and reported evidence of that committee because it is very enlightening, particularly for those hon. members who may not be familiar with the fishing industry.
I should also like to thank the minister and his home economics branch for the very fine luncheon which he tendered to that committee. The only thing that concerned me was that I noticed Newfoundland salt fish was relegated to a rather minor role on the menu. I believe this was the third time I have enjoyed a luncheon under the sponsorship of the Department of Fisheries and if my memory serves me correctly on

Supply-Fisheries
each occasion we have started out with salt fish chowder. I do hope when the next fisheries luncheon comes around Newfoundland salt cod will enjoy a much more prominent place on the menu. I would suggest to the minister that it might be worth while to have luncheons organized on a provincial basis. We could put up a very nice luncheon of. Newfoundland fish products alone and I am sure the same could be done by Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces. This would give us a chance to learn something about the fisheries not only of the east coast but of the west coast and even of the central provinces. We could have 10 luncheons a year with samples of the fisheries products from one province at each luncheon.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has already referred to the traditional importance of the Newfoundland fisheries. Historically the fishing industry has been the mainstay of the economy of Newfoundland. In the old days Newfoundland had a single crop economy based entirely on the production of salt cod. In rather recent years, as late as 1914 when world war I started, we got another basket for our eggs when we began to develop the fresh fish industry. And then, of course, as time went on the products of our forests and mines began to have more dollar value than did our fisheries but even then the fishing industry was still of major importance because it gave employment to the greatest number of people. Now that we in Newfoundland are experiencing a bit of depression, with unemployment more than double what it normally is, more and more people have been forced to return to the fisheries and so the industry is once more assuming its prominent historic importance as a major source of employment.
My friend the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare tried to make out that nothing had ever been done for the fishing industry. I would be the last to say that enough has been done for the fisheries or that as much has been done for the fisheries as for the farming industry and yet I would point out to my hon. friend that nevertheless a great deal has been done for the fishing industry. I refer him to our price supports, to the salt rebate, to fisheries loans, to insurance on lobster traps, to bounties on fishing vessels, to unemployment insurance for fishermen and, in Newfoundland, to the bait service. All of these things were done by the Liberal government. When you total them all up they constitute a substantial amount of assistance to the fishing industry although, as I said, I believe still more is required. But the tragedy of it all from my point of view is that substantial as the assistance has been very little of it has been able to trickle down

to the fisherman who is the person we really wish to help. With the exception of insurance on lobster traps and unemployment insurance practically none of this assistance has been of any material benefit to the ordinary fisherman.
I have in my hand a publication put out by the economics service of the Department of Fisheries entitled, "Operations of Modern Longliners and Draggers-Atlantic Seaboard -1957" which has been compiled by John Proskie. This is a veritable gold mine of statistical information with respect to the fishing industry. If we look through the report we find that as far as Newfoundland long-liners are concerned the break-even prices for codfish are as follows: For longliners 30 to 40 feet in length the break-even point is 1.66 cents per pound; for longliners 40 to 50 feet long the break-even point is 2.087 cents per pound; and for longliners 50 to 60 feet in length the break-even point is 2.489 cents per pound. Therefore a Newfoundland fisherman must get well over 2 cents a pound to break even on his fish.
If we look at the average fish prices for 1957 we find that the Newfoundland fisherman fishing out of a 30 to 40 foot boat received 2.08 cents per pound for codfish, which is by far the largest production of the Newfoundland fisheries. He broke even by less than half a cent a pound. The operator of a 40 to 50 foot boat did not break even. He only got 2.03 cents a pound whereas he required 2.08 cents to break even. The operator of a 50 to 60 foot boat had an even bigger deficit because he received only 2.01 cents a pound for codfish whereas he required 2.89 cents to break even.
Three days ago fish prices in Newfoundland were published in the St. John's press and looking over the Daily News of August 18 I find that the price for cod varied from If cents a pound to 2J cents a pound in the different localities throughout the island. In Englee, which is in the riding of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, they only got If cents a pound for large fish while in the first instance the If cents was for small fish. The going price for haddock three days ago was 2 cents a pound for small to 2J cents a pound for large. For rosefish, which is quite a delicacy, the price was If cents a pound for small and 2-J cents a pound for large. For flounder the price varied from 24 cents to 3 cents a pound. For halibut, which is a high-priced fish when you buy it in a store, the price varied from 10 to 12 to 15 cents a pound. These are the fish prices that were being paid in Newfoundland just three days ago.

I might point out that these prices are lower than are being paid in Norway by the fish processing plants there which I understand are not subsidized by the government. In any event, when we compare the fishing industry of Canada with that of other countries we find that the Canadian fisherman, whether he is in Newfoundland or Nova Scotia-I cannot speak about British Columbia; I believe the fishermen are all wealthy on the west coast-is worse off than his counterpart in Norway, Great Britain or the United States. In my opinion this chaotic condition is going to continue until the fishermen themselves do something about it in the same way the fishermen of Norway did. I do not think it will be sufficient for the fishermen to organize in any one province or part of a province. They will have to organize on a nationwide scale, certainly on a scale large enough to embrace all the Atlantic provinces if they are going to be able to organize their sales and get the benefit of a decent price for their fish.
The price of salt fish is always based on the price of fresh fish and is usually a little lower than that of fresh fish, particularly when you take into consideration the extra expense of buying salt and the additional work in handling the fish. We are all happy to learn that a commission is inquiring into the price spreads on fish and we hope that when their report is made it will contain concrete recommendations to show how the fisherman can get a little better price for his fish. Whether it is on the production end or on the marketing end does not matter because if the fisherman can get one cent more per pound for his fish he will be substantially better off.
Lord Bacon once said that the fisheries of Newfoundland contained more wealth than all the mines of Peru. He was probably right because the mines of Peru can be worked out but our fish resources are self-perpetuating. What we want is a little more of that wealth to trickle down to the ordinary fisherman because today he is not getting the share of that wealth to which he is entitled.

Not yet. Before I sit down I want to say a few words about the bait service. This service applies only to Newfoundland because it was one of the obligations which the federal government assumed as part of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada. We all recognize that the bait service is a very difficult service to administer and we were delighted to learn in the committee that a new portable bait freezing depot is going to be tried out, one which we understand can be built for
Supply-Fisheries
approximately $5,500, which can be added to one unit after another and which can even be moved from one place to another. That is the type of unit we need for our particular requirements in Newfoundland where the fishing industry is changing very rapidly.
Our present bait service was instituted by the Newfoundland government many years before confederation and was started as a form of insurance for the fishermen. It cost money and never paid its way but nevertheless it yielded dividends because it enabled the fisherman to produce wealth that benefited the whole province and which could never have been produced without that service. There is no use in having a bait depot unless we have bait to put in it and that is where we need a much more flexible policy than we have at the present time. The appearance of bait in Newfoundland waters is a seasonal phenomenon and it does not always come with uniform regularity. The people on the spot must have the authority to take advantage of the squid and other types of bait when they appear because the run may only last a week and then they are gone. If we do not do it they do not return and we are left without bait.
Some hon. members have referred to the fact that a great deal of our bait is sold to foreign trawlers which produce fish to compete with us in our salt fish markets. While we are anxious to co-operate as much as we possibly can with the other nations of the world, yet I think charity begins at home. We must look after the requirements of our own fishermen before we permit bait to be sold to the fishermen from other countries. I think that is fair and reasonable. I think that is what other countries would do. I am sure we would find it very difficult if we had to go to another country to buy bait for our fishermen when they did not have enough to supply their own requirements. I urge the government to look at this problem and take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that the bait requirements of our Newfoundland fishermen will be met before bait is sold to our competitors.
The bait service is important, not only for bait to catch cod, haddock and other ground fish, but it is important also to our lobster fishery. The lobster fishery is a very important fishery and one that is subject to management with resultant improved returns to the fishermen. Very often in the early part of the year our lobster fishermen are handicapped because they cannot get bait. We may not, at all times, have sufficient bait on hand to provide for that industry. Not only must we have bait, but we also must have refrigerated boats to take the bait from one large depot to another. At the moment we have only one

Supply-Fisheries
small boat which is antiquated and will soon have to be scrapped. What we need are three new ships specially built for the bait service. In the winter season particularly, when these boats cannot be used along the north shore because of ice conditions, they could very well be employed in the rescue service along the southwest coast. As the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare pointed out they are urgently needed in New Brunswick, and the need is no less urgent in Newfoundland.
With respect to the administration of the bait service, I would hope the government would give consideration to the cancellation of these leases to private interests. To my knowledge, the private firms who have leased these depots have not lived up to the terms of their agreement, and I know that a certain amount of discrimination has resulted. Fishermen in one area have an advantage which is denied to those in other areas. Furthermore, certain fishermen have not been permitted to get bait from these depots at the regular price unless they agreed to sell their fish to the person who owned the lease. This is all contrary to the original terms of the lease and I think these things would justify the cancellation of these leases which are really becoming a source of great annoyance.
The best way, in my opinion, to administer these bait depots is to put them under the local authorities. Our time in Newfoundland is about an hour and a half ahead of that of Ottawa. At 3.00 p.m. on Friday in Newfoundland it is 4.30 p.m. in Ottawa and should a problem arise by the time we get in touch with the department in Ottawa by telephone most of the officials have gone for the weekend. Then, we cannot do anything about it until Monday. If it is a long weekend, we might not be able to get in touch with them until Tuesday. During that time a lot of things could happen.
I want to give you one illustration. Last year, like this year, there was no bait late in the fall. In one particular place there did appear a school of what we call whitefish which fishermen do use as bait in an emergency. However, it happened that these white-fish were in a little arm of the bay and there was a regulation somewhere on the federal statute books which prevented the fishermen from taking those whitefish on that date because they were in that particular spot. What we wanted to do was to get permission from Ottawa to get these whitefish which were so urgently needed for bait and which are not taken for any other purpose. Ottawa was closed down for the weekend, as it was a Friday afternoon, so we could not get permission. On Tuesday the whitefish had gone and the fishermen were still without bait.

This is only one illustration. There are hundreds that could be given to emphasize the need for leaving more discretion in the hands of the people who are on the spot.
I hope that if these new bait freezers prove successful the fishermen themselves will be encouraged to own them, either on a co-operative basis or on a community basis -even by private industry. The more the fisherman can control the administration of the bait service the better for the fishermen and the better for the department because they will have less headaches with which to contend.
Before I sit down I want to mention briefly two other topics. The first topic is the continued exploration for the main school of herring. We know that the department has been carrying on this investigation for a number of years and that it is a long term operation which may last as long as 10 years. However, it is vital to the economy of Newfoundland that we discover this source of wealth as quickly as we possibly can. I urge the minister to spare no effort in intensifying this investigation as much as possible.
Then, I want to deal with the appearance of international fishing ships on our inshore fishing grounds. I believe this point was mentioned by my colleague the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador or by one of my other colleagues who spoke this evening. The bulk of our fishermen in Newfoundland are what we call inshore fishermen, which means they fish from tiny settlements in tiny boats. They go to small fishing grounds which are from 10 miles to 20 miles offshore. These fishing grounds, of course, being 20 miles off our shores are in international waters, they are outside of our territorial limits. They are small grounds, perhaps 20 miles long by 10 miles wide. The fishermen are absolutely dependent upon these grounds for their livelihood. If they cannot fish there with their equipment, they cannot fish anywhere else. If a foreign drag-ger comes and scrapes over the bottom three or four times, the fish are driven away or caught and it takes a long time before they return, perhaps three or four weeks or months. As a result of this, our fishermen are deprived of their livelihood. They suffer tremendous hardships.
The objection is not to these fishermen in these international waters. We recognize they have a right there as well as we have. However, we want them to recognize that these grounds are vital to our fishermen. What we object to is the particular kind of fishing operation they conduct, I mean drag-ger fishing. If these foreign fishermen would fish with a hook and line they would not

destroy the ground. They might catch some of the fish, but they would not drive the fish away. There is no reason why our fishermen could not' fish there as well as the Spaniard or Portuguese, if they would use a hook and line. This is a matter for international negotiation.
I hope the minister will use every available opportunity to explore what can be done to get some kind of a gentleman's agreement or some kind of understanding whereby we recognize their right to fish there and they recognize how vital these grounds are to our fishermen, and work out a sort of "live and let live" proposition whereby the grounds can be used to the mutual advantage of both foreign ships and our own.

Along with previous speakers, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the fisheries estimates in general, also as they pertain to our province, and in particular as they apply to the county of Kings which I have the honour to represent. First of all, 1 should like to pay a high tribute to the excellence of the work done by the minister and his department. I reflect his view expressed in speaking on the estimates in the last parliament that there is a great future for the fisheries industry. I might say that the amount of $17J million which is proposed to be expended in this department will no doubt be put to the very best possible use by the minister and his officials towards the further development of this very important industry.
Our island province is almost completely surrounded by good fishing grounds which can still stand a good deal of expansion. The heaviest catches landed in nearly all varieties are in Kings county, and it might be noted that almost 70 per cent of the landed value is in lobsters. To the fisherman of Prince Edward Island lobsters are what potatoes are to the farmer. They both provide a speculative high cash return.
In that regard I might mention a few considerations which have been brought to my attention by those engaged in that branch of the industry. First, inquiries have been made with regard to the possibility of establishing a lobster hatchery in our province. Second, our fishermen are very much interested in the experiments being carried out with aluminum traps and other more durable metal traps than the wooden ones more commonly used today. Third, fishermen in some of our areas are becoming more and more interested in programs of trap limitation and in several localities have expressed the wish that such a program be instituted. I realize that this must be an almost unanimous voluntary move on the part of the fishermen in the area, and
Supply-Fisheries
trust that the government would provide assistance where any group wished to proceed along these lines. I wish to bring these points to the attention of the department and I know we can expect their assistance in the satisfactory solution of the many problems related to them.
In addition to the some 2,500 fishermen using about 1,400 small-type boats, we have the dragger fleet which operates out of Souris at the eastern end of my riding and supplies the two large fish plants which operate there. The smaller-type draggers in use there have been quite successful, and it is now felt that a larger and more powerful type of dragger, which can go farther and operate in deeper waters, could also fish from this area and be a big asset in the extension and expansion of the fisheries of the northeastern section of Prince Edward Island. In this program the provincial government assists very materially, and it is hoped that there will be mutual co-operation with the federal government in doing everything possible to help in this field.
I could mention, too, the great usefulness of the public works program in our county which touches practically every fishing harbour this year. I should like to thank the Minister of Public Works and his most efficient deputy, Major General Young, for the co-operation and consideration shown to our fishermen in the planning and execution of the large public works program for our county.

race, colour, religion or other factors. I am by no means alone in deriving pleasure from the fact that whereas the first group is dwindling, the second is expanding very noticeably.
The blending of two great cultures and two fine sets of old-world traditions can give rise, in the new world, to a society which should eventually achieve a higher standard than could be hoped for with one culture and one set of traditions.
There can be no doubt that we all love our country, and want to see it prosperous. This can only come about if we have a strong feeling of national unity which we, members of the House of Commons can, I am sure, do much to foster and develop. During the second world war, many of us fought beside French Canadian regiments; I am thinking in particular of the Regiment de la Chaudiere, which formed part of the division I served in, and in which I counted many friends. Splendid soldiers they were, and fine comrades in arms.
We believe that under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), national unity has made much headway. Mr. Diefenbaker has said he has a single policy for all of Canada, and Canadians in general, and Quebecers in particular, have shown their faith in him, and have associated themselves with his sincere hope for the tightening of the links between all parts of the country so as to make Canada a greater and mightier force in all respects. Let us again do all within our power, as members of parliament, to foster and develop a deeper and stronger spirit of national unity throughout our beloved country.
Fishing was one of the first industries in the province of Quebec, and was introduced by the maritime Acadians at the very dawn of our history. Let it then be said, in all fairness, that our French-speaking fellow citizens were the joint pioneers of the fishing industry. Nor do I hesitate to say that they still play a decisive role in that industry, and will continue to work with us in co-operation and harmony, with all the zeal and skill they have shown in the past, for the expansion of this important sector of our economy.

This makes it difficult for some fishermen to recover their costs unless they have continuously high catches. In this regard more

than one packing firm has requested that additional financial allowances be provided so that more working capital would be available, thus allowing them to hol'd the pack until market conditions improve.
