speechtext:
The international aspects of the fisheries industry have been covered by previous speakers, as has also the ground-fish phase of the industry. I will not, therefore, take up the time of the committee by repeating what has already been said on these two very important matters. My remarks will be centred around the inshore fisheries in the Miramichi waters. May I broaden the scope of the rules and the terms of reference at this moment by offering my congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries on being conferred with a doctorate degree by his alma mater, Mount Allison University, on Saturday last.
I wish to express my thanks to the minister for his statement covering the activities of his department and to express the thanks of the Miramichi fishermen to the minister and to his departmental officials, both here in Ottawa and in the field, who are engaged in the administration, research, protection and marketing of fish, for their efforts in trying to solve the many problems with which the industry is faced. Not all the problems have been completely solved, but many improvements have been brought about as a result of the research and experience gained by the department and by the industry itself. This has gone a very long way toward improving the lot of the prime producer and assisting the distributors and processors.
Our fisheries are of prime importance. The opinion has been expressed that this department of government has not been given recognition in accordance with its importance to our economy and that the allotment of the public funds for the fisheries industry is insufficient to carry out services to the desired degree.
The constituency which I represent, North-umberland-Miramichi, produces many species of fish, most of which are in the delicacy class,

including lobsters, oysters, salmon, smelts, clams and quahogs besides many other species. Fishing provides a livelihood for many residents of this constituency both in the commercial and sports fishing fields. I do not intend to present a history of the Miramichi fisheries but we have had problems and some of these problems still exist. These problems bring forth divergent views from the many different classes of fishermen and from the buyers, even within the scope of the production of one specie of fish. This divergence is most prominent among those engaged in the salmon fishing industry and particularly applies to the fishing season dates for drift net, set net and fly fishing. The matters of the protection of spawning areas for the spring fishing of black salmon, the hatchery spawning of the late run salmon against the spawning of the early run salmon are among the phases over which there is no general agreement as to the best course to follow.
The chief concern of the department and of the fishing industry in general is that of conservation to make sure that in future sufficient stocks are available as is essential and desirable in respect of this valuable food product and that our fisheries are preserved in order to provide a continuing livelihood for a large segment of our population.
I would like to say a word as to the effect of the budworm spray on the fish and animal life in my constituency, which has been the cause of much concern. An adverse effect is expected to be apparent in the fish population during 1960 and 1961. While the protection of our forests is important, it is the earnest hope of all concerned that an effective spray solution can be found which will not be injurious to fish. The department's estimate that spraying may be completed this year was most welcomed information.
In July the Minister of Fisheries announced the establishment of a federal-provincial Atlantic fisheries committee to consider fisheries problems common to the five Atlantic provinces. The personnel of that committee comprises the federal deputy minister of fisheries and the deputy ministers of the provincial departments of fisheries of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. The committee will consider proposals and recommendations on fishery matters of common interest to all Atlantic provinces and will make recommendations to the respective governments for the implementation of programs and projects designed to assist in the development of methods and techniques and fishing equipment. It will study and report upon the economics of fisheries in order to ensure
Supply-Fisheries
that any proposed program of development is based upon sound principles. In that respect I trust that the fishermen's organizations will make extensive studies of their particular problems and will present their findings and recommendations to the respective provincial deputy ministers for study and action by the federal-provincial Atlantic fisheries council.
I turn now to matters which directly affect the Miramichi fisheries. Oyster fishermen of Miramichi suffered a severe loss when disease became prevalent among their oysters. Action was taken by the department in re-seeding these beds with disease-resistant oysters which were transplanted from beds in Prince Edward Island. By natural processes this disease should eventually be eliminated, likely within 20 to 25 years. By re-seeding with disease-resistant oysters it is estimated that oyster fishing can be resumed in five to eight years. In the meantime it is essential that every care and protection be afforded these transplanted oysters and that the best men available be engaged.
The Miramichi salmon fisheries consists of three types of fishing-drift-net fishing, set-net fishing and angling. There is considerable difference of opinion among these groups and some difference of opinion within each group as to the most favourable fishing dates.
Combined meetings in the past failed to bring about a mutually agreed set of fishing dates. This situation should be the subject matter of a special inquiry by a committee comprised of officials of the federal and provincial departments of fisheries, representatives of the three groups and representatives of the buyers.
The view has been expressed that the erection of a causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island across Northumberland strait will have an adverse effect on alewives fishing and will affect the fishing of some other species caught in the Miramichi waters. If the causeway is erected, every precaution should be taken to permit the natural flow of fish. Smelt fishing is a very important phase of Miramichi fisheries. These smelts rank the highest in quality. Here again there are divergent views as to the best fishing dates due to weather conditions and market conditions. Due to the change in climatic conditions over the years to milder winters, fishing off the ice has become hazardous. The ice is late in forming and after it has formed, unseasonable run-offs occur causing extensive loss and damage to nets and gear.
Requests over the years for the inclusion of smelt nets under the fishermen's indemnity insurance plan have not brought

Supply-Fisheries
about the desired results. The department's study of the situation found that no practical way can be found to assess the losses and keep the insurance premium at a moderate rate. I make a further request for continued study by the department towards setting up insurance coverage against loss of smelt nets and gear similar to that in effect for fishing boats and lobster traps. As a measure to alleviate losses it is suggested that regular surveys of ice conditions be made by helicopter through arrangements with the R.C.A.F. station at Chatham, and that an adequate warning system of sudden break-ups and run-offs of ice be set up using the local radio station and other means to warn the fishermen.
Lobster fishing is another important phase of Miramichi fisheries. The catch varies from season to season, and the catch varies each season in the different lobster areas within the Miramichi estuary. The protection of this species has been a continuing problem to some degree. Many reports are heard about undersized and berried-mother- lobsters being landed. The department is urged to concentrate its program of conservation on lobster fishing.
There is a splendid film showing the life and habits of the lobster which should be made available for all lobster fishermen to see. I made a request three or four years ago when this film was documented to have it shown in the different lobster fishing areas of the Miramichi. To date to my knowledge this had not been done. The showing of this film would, in my opinion, do more towards the conservation of lobsters than many protective measures now in force. I request the minister to arrange for the showing of this film in the Miramichi area with both English and French commentaries available as required.
A practical change was made this year in lobster fishing district No. 8. The hour set for fishermen to leave shore to set their traps was advanced from 12 o'clock noon to 10 o'clock a.m. I have not seen a copy of the change in regulations. However, I trust the change will apply to district 7B next year.
In the field of fly fishing many reports are heard about wholesale slaughter of fish. Reports state that fishing parties go to the headwaters of the rivers and streams and illegally net fish on their way to the spawning grounds. It is alleged that fishing parties take canning outfits into the woods and can their illegal catches on the spot. If there is any truth in these reports-and it is claimed that fish and game protective associations have certain facts-then consideration should

be given, following investigation, to closing off the spawning areas and other areas where this kind of illegal fishing is engaged in.
In the matter of salmon protection on the southwest and northwest branches of the Miramichi river and for certain other tributaries, opinions have been widely expressed that adequate protection is not provided, particularly at vulnerable periods. Protective measures are governed by the amount of money available, an economy restriction which is recognized. However, it might well be that this economy is defeating in no small measure the salmon conservation program. The Miramichi commercial salmon fishermen's association, the local fish and game protective association, and the Miramichi salmon angling association have raised this matter many times over the years. It is suggested that the minister have a complete investigation made at which time all data be collected, following which the whole field of protection can be re-assessed to ascertain if more protective measures are required for the Miramichi river and its branches to assist the Atlantic salmon conservation plan.
In the matter of providing facilities for commercial fishing, there has been much dissatisfaction expressed about the basis that is used in deciding if the construction of facilities are to be authorized. The decision is made by the economic study branch of the Department of Public Works. The decision is made solely on the amount and landed value of the fish taken at the respective area. The department of fisheries supplies the data on the fish catch and in most cases makes no further representations. It is my contention that other factors should be seriously considered and have a bearing on the decision to construct facilities such as wharves, breakwaters, small landings, extensions to existing facilities and also dredging. The reason why the landed value and size of the catch is not higher is due in large measure to the lack of facilities. These other factors concern the human energy that must be expended by the fishermen, due to lack of facilities to land their catches ashore, protection needed for boats and gear against storms, distance from existing facilities and distance from the fishermen's homes to the existing facilities.
Some of the smaller fishing areas of the Miramichi area are without facilities of any kind and catches must be man-handled to the shore and taken to the nearest access road or some considerable distances over water. The Department of Fisheries should make the decision as to the need of facilities for the fishermen, keeping in mind the hardships

faced and the benefits that would be gained in preserving the quality of the fish and increasing the volume and landed value.
The selection of personnel as fisheries officers on a permanent basis comes under the civil service commission with veterans preference recognition. This same recognition should be standard procedure for non-civil service appointments, other qualifications being equal. For seasonal employment such as patrol service and guardians, experience should be the prime qualification. To build up an adequate protective and conservation service and as a reward for good services rendered in the past, personnel who satisfactorily performed past services should be re-engaged. With regard to salaries paid seasonal and part-time fisheries employees, an increase is warranted. They should be paid on a par with comparable work at the existing prevailing wage rate.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I again suggest that the Department of Fisheries should be raised to a higher level of importance among the departments of government and that a larger share of the public funds be allotted to carry out in a fuller measure the duties of this most important branch so necessary to our economy and vital to the livelihood of those Canadians who toil the hardest for the smallest remuneration.

Mr. Chairman, on an earlier occasion in this house I took the opportunity of expressing my views on the fishing industry in Newfoundland and the problems facing the industry in that province. It is not my intention to repeat those statements at this time. I do not wish to unduly delay the passage of the minister's estimates but I do wish to make a few brief remarks.
First of all, I should like to commend the minister for the excellent work that was carried out by him during the discussion of his estimates in the standing committee. I appreciate the fact that he was present at all meetings of the committee and gave of his knowledge in answering the questions that were put to him. I take that as a measure of his interest in the department which he heads, an interest which I believe augurs well for the future of the fishing industry in Canada. And while I wish to offer the minister my congratulations for his work and also to extend congratulations to the officials of his department and the chairman of the standing committee I wish also to extend my very personal congratulations to the minister for the honour which was conferred on him last Saturday by his own university, Mount Allison.
I believe that if the fishing industry of Newfoundland is to take a prominent place

among the primary industries in Canada some price supports will be needed for the produce of the industry. I believe, too, that if we are going to maintain our markets for particular types of produce, such as light salt fish, or to provide a type of fish that is required by a certain market it may be necessary not only to provide further price supports but to provide a bonus for products that will be acceptable in the various markets of the world. I would suggest to the minister that very serious consideration be given to this problem.
Within the last few days we have heard that the exporting association responsible for exporting Newfoundland fish, an association commonly known as NAFEL, is reaching the end of its life and has only another year to operate. I would hope by the time the present year has expired and NAFEL is no longer an exporting association for Newfoundland fish there will be provided by the federal government some form of association, commission or board that will bring some order to the marketing of fisheries products in the province of Newfoundland. When I refer to the marketing of fisheries products I do not mean only the actual marketing process within the province itself but also the marketing processes that take place in the markets of the world. While I am not here making any plea for NAFEL I do indeed make a plea for some organization that will take its place when NAFEL no longer exists.
It is indeed somewhat difficult to discuss the fisheries industry in Newfoundland without discussing as well the facilities which aid the fishermen to carry on their work.
I know the estimates of the Minister of Public Works have already been passed but I should like to make a brief reference to them and say that on the section of the coast which I represent we have some harbours that are large and some that are small and on straight shore. We still need a great many structures for the protection of fishing equipment such as small private wharves and fishing boats. I hope that in large areas where a considerable quantity of fish is produced such as in St. George's bay the time will not be too far distant when we can have those facilities that will enable the fishermen to carry on their work in the way in which they would like to carry it on.
Reference has been made a number of times today to a problem that exists in my province and it is so serious in the riding I have the honour to represent that I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without making a few brief comments concerning it.

Supply-Fisheries
I refer, of course, to the need for an expanded bait service. I appreciate that the minister and his officials have been making a very serious study of this problem in Newfoundland. I know, too, they have come up with a solution which they are hoping to conduct on an experimental basis. This bait service is of extreme importance to the fishermen who live along the coast. In the first place it enables them to get to work earlier in the year and it enables them to fish longer during the season with the result that their productivity is increased. It also enables them to increase their annual earnings so they can raise the level of their income to a status more comparable with wages earned in other industries. In addition to this it provides employment in Newfoundland at a time when in various other fields employment is not as plentiful as it was a year ago.
I hope the experiment which the minister intends to conduct in the province of Newfoundland shortly will be productive of worth-while results. I have already suggested to him several places where the bait service should be expanded and I shall now give him another list and suggest to him that bait depots should be provided for the following places: Codroy, St. George's bay, Port-au-Port bay, bay of Islands, Bonne Bay, Cow Head, Daniel's Harbour, the St. Barbe area and the Flower's Cove area. Along that coast it is a distance of 300 miles in a straight line but more nearly 1,000 miles by following the coastline and on that whole coastline there is but one bait depot in a distance of approximately 1,000 miles. It is not possible for these men to carry on their industry, an industry from which they could make a good living, without being able to obtain the bait so necessary to them. I hope that the minister will continue to give very serious consideration to this problem, as I know he has already.
During the proceedings of the standing committee the minister was not able to provide us with the number of freezing units that would be built nor was he in a position then to give us the locations of these units. When the particular item is before the committee later in the discussion I hope the minister will be able to give us that information. I have a number of questions but I shall present them to the minister when the various items are before the committee.

I want to say just a word about the bait situation. I must say I was very pleased indeed by the announcement made by the minister concerning these improvements that he is hoping to effect in the bait distribution situation in Newfoundland. I do hope that when he is putting in all these bait depots in the riding of Humber-St. George's, he will not forget one or two for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. I should like to put forward a special word for Herring Neck.
The situation in Newfoundland this year is that if we had a lot of bait depots there would not be bait to put in many of them. I know the minister is doing his best in the circumstances to try to meet that situation, but the situation is really a desperate one. We have had a poor fishery up to now. If there is not bait available for the fall fishery, even if the fish are plentiful, then the fall fishery is going to be poorer because of the shortage of bait. I do urge the minister, in every possible way he can devise, to do what he can to meet this emergency situation. I appeal to him also to try to take steps to foresee it and to meet it ahead of time. I know there have been difficulties this year. I certainly do not want to suggest the government has any responsibility for them because they have not, but I do urge the greatest possible zeal, which I am sure there will be, in trying to meet this very serious problem.
There are just two other topics that I want to mention. One topic about which I want to say a word or two is the marketing situation. I know the minister could rise on a point of order and say that he is not responsible for marketing fish but that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is. I do not believe the minister will rise on any such point of order, and for this reason: We look to the Minister of Fisheries to look after the interests of the fishermen and the fishing industry. We look to him to urge his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and his other colleagues to consider that this industry more than any other, more than the pulp and paper industry, more than the wheat industry, is an industry that depends upon exports for its life. There is no other industry that exports as large a proportion of its product as the cod fishery
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
of Canada. I do believe things could be done to increase the market in Canada. I have made suggestions to the minister in that respect which I am not going to repeat now.
We have been very upset indeed, not only in Newfoundland but all along the Atlantic coast, at the loss of the Jamaican market. It is a very serious blow indeed to have a substantial portion of our total lost to someone else who has never supplied it before, especially when we know that the Icelanders are selling fish that is subsidized to an inordinate degree. Yesterday or the day before we heard over the radio that the Russian government is lending the Icelandic authorities $3.5 million with which to build more fishing boats to compete to an even greater extent with our unsubsidized fishery. This is a problem that just cannot be allowed to drift. At the same time we know, as the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador pointed out earlier, that we provide a market for Jamaican goods which is two or three times as large as the market for Canadian goods in Jamaica. It is difficult to understand why it is not possible for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to do more than has been done to get this market back. We do hope the Minister of Fisheries will never let him rest, that he will be at him every day and at his officers.
I am going to say again that I am not going to trespass on your patience very much longer. I view with the gravest alarm this increase in the wool tariff, not so much the tariff against Britain in this respect as the threat of an increased tariff against Italy which is the best market we have in Europe for our fish. It is a very, very dangerous thing, even to be threatening to do. I do hope that all those members from fishing ridings who sit on the other side will make their views known to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister, and urge them on no account to proceed with this folly, because folly it would certainly be, and worse, for the fishing industry.
I do want to say, in that particular context, that I was rather astonished at the answer given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to a question the other day concerning what was to replace NAFEL. The question was asked by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception and the reply is found in Hansard for August 16, page 3650. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that this was not just a federal problem but was a provincial problem as well. I do not know where the Minister of Trade and Commerce got his constitutional advice, but I would suggest he read the British North America

Act again. He will find that this is exclusively a federal responsibility, and it is an inescapable federal responsibility. It is not good enough to revoke the licence of NAFEL and put nothing in its place. If we go back to the cut-throat competition that existed before NAFEL, the whole fishing industry is going to be in chaos in a very short time. Something has got to be done, a lead has to be given by the government in this matter. I do not believe any steps will be taken unless the Minister of Fisheries takes the lead in the government. It is for this reason that I, like other members from Newfoundland, appeal to him so strongly to do something.
There is just one other point on which I should like to say a word. This is the one fly in the ointment so far as the minister is concerned. He would not expect, especially being the Minister of Fisheries, that there would not be a fly somewhere. There is one small fly in the ointment. I have here in my hand a copy of an editorial which appeared in the St. John's Evening Telegram. of May 16, 1958, which is very appropriately entitled "Wrong Party". I am not going to read the whole of it, but I should like to read an extract as follows:
A number of river wardens (or rather, a number of people who WERE river wardens) have been kicking like mules this spring because the federal government appointed a number of new wardens who are not natural-born Liberals. The ex-wardens who have been putting up the beef say that some of the wardens appointed this spring may actually be Conservative sympathizers, and they have been writing nasty letters about it to St. John's and Ottawa-
Some of the ex-wardens have even written Mr. Pickersgill demanding their old jobs back. They obviously think the Liberals are still in power, and aren't aware of the fact that it is Mr. Jed Winter, the DEFEATED (Tory) candidate, who now appoints river wardens in the district of Bonavista-Twillin-gate, not Mr. Pickersgill, whom these people elected to sit in opposition. Talk about the Age of Innocence.
When the minister gets up to speak, I know that he is going to tell us that Mr. Winter has no more to do with the appointment of these river wardens or guardians than I have. I trust he will give them and me that assurance in a completely unqualified fashion. I am one of those innocents who would expect that to be the case. I have listened to the professions made by the house leader over and over again as he beat his breast, and I cannot believe there is any truth in this editorial. I must say I had a slight suspicion there might be when the official agent, not of Mr. Jed Winter but of the Tory candidate who ran against me in 1957, became a river warden. But I suppose that was a pure coincidence, and I understand that he has since resigned.
Supply-Fisheries
Speaking seriously, I believe there are two considerations that ought to be kept in mind about these river guardians, if they have done their jobs well. Most of them were people who, in the nature of things, were not very well qualified for other types of occupation or they would have had other jobs in the days of the full employment we had in Newfoundland when the Liberals were in office. I suggest that the minister should make a special effort to appoint as wardens or guardians, as I think is the correct term, men who are veterans and who are perhaps slightly disabled and therefore not able to do more strenuous work so well. But above all, I think he should give the preference to people who really cannot leave home to work and who badly need the work. If he does find a few Tories here and there in Bonavista-Twillingate, as long as that is not the prime qualification, it will be all right with me. I certainly never inquired of anyone who ever came to me asking for assistance and looking for work who he had voted for.

speechtext:
One question that has been uppermost in the minds of many of the members of the committee who spoke this afternoon and this evening is that of guaranteeing or seeing to it, if possible, that the primary producer in the fishing industry gets a reasonable return for his labours. Attempts are being made in that direction. One of them has already been referred to, the royal commission on price spreads. The item having to do with that was dealt with in the items under privy council this afternoon.

Supply-Fisheries
There is the question of price support. I should like to point out that there is in existence a Fisheries Prices Support Act that is functioning or is there to function whenever it is considered necessary that price support be provided. This act allows price support, using the term in a general sense, to be provided by various means such as mass purchases when there is overproduction, deficiency payments and other ways. I called together the fisheries price support board for a meeting not very long ago. They met here in Ottawa and adjourned to meet again on September 6, I believe in Halifax, and again two days later in St. John's, Newfoundland, for the purpose of considering the situation of the market for salt cod, because that is the only segment of the industry at the moment that has made a formal request for the consideration of price support.
As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has pointed out, there are in this matter complications or difficulties that make a floor price for fish even more difficult a matter than it is for some other products because, as has been pointed out by many members of the committee, a very large percentage of our fish is exported and our market depends on export for the great majority of our production. There is the danger that with anything that might be a subsidy or a price support, there is always a certain amount of risk of retaliatory tariff action by other countries or similar action.
The hon. member for Gloucester mentioned the inspection service. I want to say briefly that we are working hard at extending that service and making it more efficient. In the not too distant future we hope to have inspection compulsory for fresh fish and frozen fillets right throughout the country as is now the case with so many other products.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare and I think the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo mentioned the necessity for something approaching a mother ship for fishing fleets, some ship provided at the taxpayers' expense which would be there to render assistance of any sort necessary to the fishing fleet in a given area. This is a suggestion that I welcome and this matter is being given study. An over-all fourth service such as that in the United States-a full-blown coastguard as such-would entail tremendous expense. However, I think there is progress that can be made in further co-ordination of the efforts of the services that are already available, such as the navy, the air force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and perhaps augmented, if we can afford it, by some special vessels of some sort which might be operated by the Department of Fisheries itself.

Then there is a matter that I think was mentioned by all the members from Newfoundland who spoke. It is one of great concern, namely the shortage of bait or bait service generally in Newfoundland. Over the last number of years the department has tended, in my opinion, to err somewhat in the direction of being too careful in their expenditures with regard to this service in one connection, namely carrying large quantities of herring bait as a reserve. In a good year, when the squid come in, the herring is not considered the best possible type of bait and the fishermen will not buy it. The department is then left with a large quantity of bait on its hands for which it can get little or nothing. It may recover something by reducing this bait to fish meal. But if it is in an isolated place, it is not even worth transporting it to a reduction plant and it is a complete waste. I think the department has perhaps been a little too zealous in this direction through fear of criticisms which might be made of the department on account of potential waste in this direction.
I take the attitude that there should always be a reasonable reserve in case the squid, which is the most desirable bait, does not migrate to the shores of Newfoundland in any particular season and I would be prepared if the squid did arrive to defend the loss, whatever it might be, that the taxpayers might suffer as a result of having to dump supplies of herring which were no longer useful for bait. I might say we have at present being delivered 125,000 pounds of herring and 50,000 pounds of mackerel for use as bait in Newfoundland, which we have procured in the maritimes, and that there will be further supplies. We hope that the situation will be further relieved if the squid show up.
Something has been said about exploratory fishing and the necessity for this type of project. I welcome the suggestions in this connection but I would like to say that the department is now making efforts in this connection and has been doing so for a number of years. For example, at the present time there is exploratory fishing for herring, scallops and shrimps in Newfoundland. In Prince Edward Island exploratory fishing is being done for quahaugs, a type of clam, and in Nova Scotia a demonstration of the Danish seining out of Cheticamp will commence very shortly, while at the present time in New Brunswick demonstration and experimental work of the mid-water trawl is now in progress and will continue as long as it is considered desirable for it to do so. In Quebec there is exploratory fishing for herring at the present time in co-operation with the government of Quebec and the

mid-water trawl experiments in New Brunswick are also being carried out with the co-operation of the provincial government there. I might say in that connection that many of the most profitable scallop beds which are now being fished commercially on a large scale have been discovered by exploratory fishing and that the exploratory fishing for herring is a long-term program over a number of years. It is a process of elimination until we find the mother lode, as it were, of the great resources of herring available on the east coast generally.
The hon. member for Skeena made some remarks concerning the question of fish versus power. This expression does not particularly appeal to me because my hope is that it will never become a case of fish or power but that rather it will be a case of fish and power so far as that is feasible. His comments in this direction follow very closely the attitude of myself and of the department generally, which is one of developing power where such supplies exist and where they do not interfere with fish, and for as much research work to be done as possible to try to find the means of developing power and having fish even on fish streams and also conducting experimental work to provide artificial spawning beds besides any other program which has some hope of success.
The hon. member for Skeena also inquired about the north Pacific fisheries treaty and as to what is the position regarding this treaty which is in effect a treaty between the United States, Japan and ourselves. Furthermore, he inquired as to whether or not Canadian fish are being fished by the Japanese on the high seas. All I can say in that regard is that we have not one shred of evidence so far to indicate that fish originating in Canada are being caught on the high seas by the Japanese west of the parallel 175 degrees west, which is a provisional dividing line between the waters fished by the Japanese on the one side of the Pacific and the United States and ourselves on the other. Means of determining the migration of Pacific salmon are not limited to the tagging of salmon, although this is one of the important aspects. There are other aspects also; there is scientific research into parasites with which these salmon are infested, depending on where they come from, and it is possible scientifically to determine the origin of the fish from the type of parasite to which he happens to be host. There are minute differences in the structure of the fish originating on the opposite sides of the Pacific and there are oceanographic studies which indicate to a fairly accurate degree
Supply-Fisheries
the distribution of salmon. As further research is done in this connection this may prove to be the main means of determining the distribution of this fish.
I want to refer very briefly to the fact that there is a co-ordinating committee, as has been mentioned, set up on the official level between the five Atlantic provinces and the federal government, especially having to do with the problems that affect fishing in that part of Canada. We also have a committee to deal with the question of subsidies to longliner and dragger types of vessels, and this method is being studied very carefully. It is a fairly complicated problem because the cost of the vessel does not go up in direct proportion to its tonnage. Costs generally have gone up and there have been requests on the one hand for a subsidy on sizes smaller than is presently the case and at the other end of the scale it has been recommended that a subsidy be paid on the larger sizes because they are more efficient and economical. However, this matter is under very careful study and there will be adjustments which we hope will make improvements in that connection.
The hon. member for Gloucester mentioned the question of the opening of the lobster season, and I am happy to advise him that it has already been moved ahead two hours from 12 o'clock noon to 10 o'clock, which we hope will solve the problem.

That in effect will be the case, yes, and this is especially important for these fishermen in the maritimes, the majority of whom are very careful Sabbath keepers and are faced with the situation that the season opens on a Monday and they have to put out their traps on the Saturday, whereas some of their neighbours can continue to do so all day Sunday to the detriment of those who keep the Sabbath. That is only by way of interjection, however, and the problem is in effect that unless the fishermen are allowed to put out their traps as early as possible in the day they may not finish their operations before dark, especially at this time of the year and later on when the days are shorter.
Some very good suggestions were made regarding consumer services and our advertising programs and other means of stimulating greater consumption of fish by the Canadian people. I might say that we are doing what we consider to be a very good job in this connection through advertising, movies, demonstrations, publications, through our dieticians, etc. I may say that our advertising budget is very limited, but we try to squeeze the last cent of benefit out of it in order to

Supply-Fisheries
try to familiarize Canadians to a greater extent with the benefits of having more fish in their diets. This has been true of the department over the years, so much so that virtually not one cent of money is spent in blowing our own horn, or trying to bring the work that is being done by the ministry to the attention of the public generally. Maybe this is so to a fault.
There is a story in this connection which I think may have some bearing on this. It is said that at one time there was a poor widow in the maritimes who had two sons. One went to sea and the other became minister of fisheries, and neither one of them was ever heard of again.
Several members brought up the question of the importance of international trade as it relates to the fishing industry, and I want to say that this is something which I realize to be of primary importance, because it is of no use to produce fish efficiently if we cannot sell them. I will bring the suggestions which various members have made to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I will certainly keep a very careful watching brief.

The first was whether he is able to indicate what results, if any, have arisen out of the deliberations of the committee of the Pacific salmon fisheries commission which is meeting in Hawaii, or which began its meetings a couple of weeks ago, and whether he has any knowledge of what the committee discussed and decided. The other point was

whether he is in a position to make any announcement with respect to the information garnered by our Canadian research vessels which are apparently going to cover areas in the Pacific which have not been covered before.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Regarding the first question, I want to say that the meeting in Hawaii is a meeting of an ad hoc subcommittee set up to study research information which is now available, prior to the regular meeting which will be held in Tokyo and which may go on into November.
With regard to the other question I may say that so far as the north Pacific salmon fisheries commission is concerned the three nations do not operate separately; their efforts are pooled and programs are allocated by the commission itself with regard to the areas in which they operate. The primary information which is gained is made available immediately to the parties concerned, but in a case where the scientists of one country happen to be doing research with regard to a particular topic which has been allocated to them they do not wish to make their conclusions known from the information which has been gained until they are as sure as they can be that their conclusions are valid.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: There is another point bearing on that. Could the minister indicate from past experience of the operation of these research vessels how long it may take before this information is available? Would it be this year, or this season?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
This particular vote contains an item in connection with the attempt to discover means of combatting lampreys in the great lakes and to stamp them out, and since the minister is going to undertake to go after one of his colleagues I should like to give him another minister to go after in the interests of large numbers of fishermen on the north shore of lake Superior who are directly affected by this menace and at the present time, because of regulations under the unemployment insurance commission, are not able to take advantage of unemployment insurance benefits because they do not have face to face dealings but arms length dealings with their outlets in the United States and Montreal.
I would ask the minister in connection with this difficulty if he could not make some representations to the Minister of Labour, and if one of his officials or inspectors could not visit this area and get into the human side as it concerns the fishermen at Port Coldwell and Rossport, particularly, and also, to a certain extent at the lakehead. I have heard some comments tonight, especially from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, about the need for the Atlantic fishermen to get some of the things which have been given to the western farmers.
The Atlantic fishermen are getting a great deal more in terms of government support than are our great lakes fishermen. In addition to that, as far as I know, the cod is still running which is more than one can say for the lake trout in lake Superior. 1 wanted to ask the minister if he could not find out more 57071-3-249
Supply-Fisheries
about the problems of great lakes fishermen from the human side. I should also like to know what progress has been made in cleaning up the lamprey eel menace and beyond that what the program will be for restocking the fish in lake Superior?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the first question raised by the hon. member I shall certainly have the matter looked into and I shall also bring it to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Labour.
Regarding the progress in trying to find ways of eliminating the lamprey menace in the great lakes, as the committee knows this program is carried on by the international great lakes fisheries commission. The research board is Canada's agent for doing the research aspect of the work in this connection. Canada's contribution to that work this year in terms of dollars is $470,000 which is 31 per cent of the entire cost. The United States contributes the other 69 per cent.
All major lamprey streams on lake Superior on both the Canadian and United States sides have electric lamprey barriers in operation at the present time. There are larger numbers of lampreys being killed this year by this means than ever before. United States scientists have been able to discover a chemical which is a lamprecide or, in other words, a chemical that will kill lampreys. It will kill them in the larvae stage as well as at maturity. This has great promise but it will be an expensive proposition and is still in the experimental stage. However, it has the advantage of being able to kill lamprey back to the larvae stage whereas supposing you succeeded in killing all the mature lamprey, you would still have to go for five years until the larvae matured before you would have them all.
The restocking is not a major problem in lake superior because there are sufficient stocks remaining in the lakes and naturally they will rapidly multiply and re-establish the lake trout stock there providing the lampreys can be destroyed.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the minister's notice the feeling of fishermen in the area concerning the reduction in quantities of trout. I do not know if there is any real empirical basis to the idea they have but many people feel one of the factors that has not been considered yet in research into the disappearance of the lake trout and its great reduction in numbers is the tremendous growth of the smelt run in lake Superior and the competition this provides for the lake trout. I do not know whether there is any real basis for it or not and I should appreciate hearing whether any

Supply-Fisheries
study has been made of this question and if the problem could be attacked from that angle because it is one of the factors which tends to contribute to the pessimism of the people engaged in fisheries in that area.

564. To provide lor the destruction of dogfish and other predators, $250,000.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could give us an indication, Mr. Chairman, of what efforts have been expended to attempt to eliminate dogfish or to decrease their numbers?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: This is a considerable problem, Mr. Chairman. In past years there was a method devised which did not work out satisfactorily. Under this method a subsidy was paid on dogfish or dogfish livers. We are contemplating trying direct destruction of the dogfish, fishing for them directly and killing them, to see if this will give a reasonable return for the cost involved. In the meantime we are contemplating other possibilities as well. One of my senior officials is going out to British Columbia in the immediate future to make sure we are not missing a good bet in adopting some effective method which might be used. He will be talking to those engaged in the industry and fishermen to obtain their suggestions.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I believe it has been the suggestion of fishermen themselves that an attempt be made to deal with the dogfish as predators and to eliminate them by direct destruction. That was the only solution they could envisage as being practical. Is it the intention to have higher votes for conducting this program?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: That is our present intention. It will be done in an experimental way. It may prove too costly for the results that are obtained but that will be our initial approach to the problem.
Item agreed to.
